questions.title: Lecture 4–5 Extra MC · Autumn 2017 P1
questions.promptMarkdown: We want to buy a contract which gives us an annual payment of $215\,000$ forever, with first payment two years from now. What is fair price for the contract if the discount rate is $10\%$?
rubricChecks: Set up the deferred infinite geometric series starting at t = 2
Evaluate the perpetuity sum 215000 / ((1 + r) * r) at r = 0.10 to obtain 1,954,545
hints: Hint 1: A perpetuity with first payment $C$ at $t=1$ has present value $C/r$ (Ch. 4). Here the first payment arrives at $t=2$, so it is discounted one extra year.
Hint 2: Write $\text{PV} = \frac{215\,000}{(1+r)^2} + \frac{215\,000}{(1+r)^3} + \cdots = \frac{215\,000}{(1+r)r}$ and substitute $r = 0.10$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
The present value of the cash flow is the infinite geometric series with first term $a_1 = \frac{215\,000}{(1+r)^2}$ and common ratio $k = \frac{1}{1+r}$:
$$\text{PV} = \frac{215\,000}{(1+r)^2} + \frac{215\,000}{(1+r)^3} + \cdots = \frac{a_1}{1-k} = \frac{\frac{215\,000}{(1+r)^2}}{1 - \frac{1}{1+r}} = \frac{215\,000}{(1+r)r}$$
With $r = 0.10$:
$$\text{PV} = \frac{215\,000}{1.10 \cdot 0.10} = \frac{215\,000}{0.11} \approx 1\,954\,545$$
This lies between $1\,800\,000$ and $2\,000\,000$, so **C** is correct.
questions.pitfall: Using $C/r = 215\,000 / 0.10 = 2\,150\,000$ directly forgets that the first payment is at $t=2$ rather than $t=1$.

questions.title: Lecture 4–5 Extra MC · Autumn 2017 P2
questions.promptMarkdown: We want to buy a contract which gives us an annual payment forever, with first payment two years from now. The payment after two years is $390\,000$ and each year the payment is increased by $4\%$. What is fair price for the contract if the discount rate is $10\%$?
rubricChecks: Identify first term a1 = 390000/(1+r)^2 and ratio k = 1.04/(1+r) with |k| < 1
Simplify PV = 390000 / ((1+r)(r - 0.04)) and compute 5,909,091 at r = 0.10
hints: Hint 1: Model the growing perpetuity as an infinite geometric series with first term at $t=2$ and annual growth factor $1+g = 1.04$ (Ch. 4).
questions.solutionMarkdown:
The present value is the infinite geometric series:
$$\text{PV} = \frac{390\,000}{(1+r)^2} + \frac{390\,000 \cdot 1.04}{(1+r)^3} + \cdots = \frac{\frac{390\,000}{(1+r)^2}}{1 - \frac{1.04}{1+r}} = \frac{390\,000}{(1+r)(r - 0.04)}$$
Substituting $r = 0.10$ gives:
$$\text{PV} = \frac{390\,000}{1.10 \cdot 0.06} = \frac{390\,000}{0.066} \approx 5\,909\,091$$
Hence the fair price is between $5\,000\,000$ and $6\,000\,000$, so **B** is correct.
questions.pitfall: Applying Gordon's formula $390\,000/(0.10-0.04) = 6\,500\,000$ gives the value at $t=1$, forgetting to divide by $1.10$ to discount back to $t=0$.

questions.title: Lecture 4–5 Extra MC · Autumn 2017 P3
questions.promptMarkdown: An annuity loan of $300\,000$ has $14.40\%$ nominal interest, monthly payment and compounding and should be repaid in $5$ years. What share of the borrowed amount is the total interest?
rubricChecks: Convert nominal 14.40% to monthly rate r_m = 1.2% and n = 60 monthly terms
Solve the annuity PV equation for monthly payment A = 7042.84
Compute total interest share (60A - 300000)/300000 = 40.9%
hints: Hint 1: First find the monthly interest rate $r_m = \frac{14.40\%}{12} = 1.2\% = 0.012$ and total number of payments $n = 5 \cdot 12 = 60$ (Ch. 4).
questions.solutionMarkdown:
With monthly rate $r = \frac{0.144}{12} = 0.012$ and $n = 5 \cdot 12 = 60$ payments of $A$, the loan equation is:
$$\frac{A}{1.012} + \frac{A}{1.012^2} + \cdots + \frac{A}{1.012^{60}} = \frac{A}{1.012^{60}} \cdot \frac{1.012^{60}-1}{0.012} = 300\,000$$
Solving for $A$:
$$A = \frac{300\,000 \cdot 1.012^{60} \cdot 0.012}{1.012^{60} - 1} \approx 7\,042.84$$
Total interest divided by the principal is:
$$\frac{60 \cdot 7\,042.84 - 300\,000}{300\,000} \approx 0.4086 = 40.9\%$$
Since $40.9\% > 40\%$, **A** is correct.
questions.pitfall: Dividing total interest by total payments $60A$ instead of the borrowed principal $300\,000$ gives $29\%$ and leads to trap C.

questions.title: Lecture 4–5 Extra MC · Autumn 2017 P4
questions.promptMarkdown: We invest $3\,000\,000$ and expect the investment to give a payment of $150\,000$ after two years and then everlasting annual payments which increases with an annual growth factor of $1+g$. The discount rate is $r = 10\%$. Which statement is true?
options: The investment is profitable if $g = 6\%$, but not if $g = 5\%$.
The investment is profitable if $g = 5\%$, but not if $g = 6\%$.
The investment is not profitable if $g = 7\%$.
rubricChecks: Sum the infinite series for g < r = 0.10 to PV = 150000 / ((1+r)(r - g))
Set PV >= 3,000,000 at r = 0.10 and solve for break-even growth g = 0.10 - 1/22 ≈ 5.45%
hints: Hint 1: Express the present value of the future inflows for $g < r$ as $\text{PV} = \frac{150\,000}{(1+r)(r-g)}$ and compare with the initial outlay $3\,000\,000$ (Ch. 4).
Hint 2: Solve $\frac{150\,000}{1.10(0.10 - g)} = 3\,000\,000$ for the threshold growth rate $g$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
For $g < r = 0.10$, the present value of the future inflows is the infinite geometric series:
$$\text{PV} = \frac{150\,000}{(1+r)^2} + \frac{150\,000(1+g)}{(1+r)^3} + \cdots = \frac{150\,000}{(1+r)(r-g)}$$
Setting $\text{PV} = 3\,000\,000$ at $r = 0.10$:
$$\frac{150\,000}{1.10(0.10 - g)} = 3\,000\,000 \implies \frac{1}{0.10 - g} = \frac{1.10 \cdot 3\,000\,000}{150\,000} = 22$$
Thus $0.10 - g = \frac{1}{22} \approx 0.04545$, giving break-even growth $g = 0.10 - \frac{1}{22} \approx 5.45\%$. Since higher $g$ raises PV, the investment is profitable when $g \ge 5.45\%$ (hence profitable at $6\%$, not at $5\%$). **B** is correct.
questions.pitfall: Forgetting the $(1+r) = 1.10$ factor in the denominator gives break-even $g = 5.0\%$ instead of $5.45\%$, flipping the conclusion at $g=5\%$.

questions.title: Lecture 4–5 Extra MC · Spring 2018 P1
questions.promptMarkdown: We want to buy a contract which gives us an annual payment of $230\,000$ forever, with first payment three years from now. Fair price equals the present value of the cash flow. What is fair price for the contract if the discount rate is $10\%$?
rubricChecks: Set up infinite geometric series starting at t = 3: a1 = 230000/(1+r)^3
hints: Hint 1: A perpetuity starting at $t=3$ has present value $230\,000/r$ evaluated at $t=2$, so discount twice more to reach $t=0$ (Ch. 4).
Hint 2: Compute $\text{PV} = \frac{230\,000}{(1+r)^2 r}$ with $r = 0.10$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
The present value is the infinite geometric series starting at $t=3$:
$$\text{PV} = \frac{230\,000}{(1+r)^3} + \frac{230\,000}{(1+r)^4} + \cdots = \frac{230\,000}{(1+r)^2 r}$$
With $r = 0.10$:
$$\text{PV} = \frac{230\,000}{1.10^2 \cdot 0.10} = \frac{230\,000}{0.121} \approx 1\,900\,826$$
This lies between $1\,800\,000$ and $2\,000\,000$, so **C** is correct.
questions.pitfall: Discounting by $(1+r)^3$ instead of $(1+r)^2$ after dividing by $r$ undercounts one year and drops the value to $1\,728\,024$ (trap B).

questions.title: Lecture 4–5 Extra MC · Spring 2018 P4
questions.promptMarkdown: We invest $3\,000\,000$ and expect the investment to give a payment of $150\,000$ after two years and then annual payments which increase with $5\%$ each year. The discount rate is $r$. Which statement is true?
options: The investment is profitable if $r = 15\%$, but not if $r = 10\%$.
The investment is profitable if $r = 10\%$, but not if $r = 15\%$.
The investment is profitable if $r = 8\%$, but not if $r = 10\%$.
The investment is not profitable if $r = 10\%$, but not if $r = 8\%$.
rubricChecks: Sum the series for r > 0.05 to PV(r) = 150000 / ((1+r)(r - 0.05))
Set PV(r) = 3,000,000 to get r^2 + 0.95r - 0.10 = 0 and find IRR r ≈ 9.56%
hints: Hint 1: For $r > 0.05$, the infinite geometric series sums to $\text{PV}(r) = \frac{150\,000}{(1+r)(r - 0.05)}$ (Ch. 3–4).
Hint 2: Either test $r = 0.08$ and $r = 0.10$ directly in $\text{PV}(r) > 3\,000\,000$, or solve $(1+r)(r-0.05) = 0.05$ for the IRR.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
For $r > 0.05$, the present value of the inflows is:
$$\text{PV}(r) = \frac{150\,000}{(1+r)^2} + \frac{150\,000 \cdot 1.05}{(1+r)^3} + \cdots = \frac{150\,000}{(1+r)(r - 0.05)}$$
Setting $\text{PV}(r) = 3\,000\,000$ gives $(1+r)(r - 0.05) = \frac{150\,000}{3\,000\,000} = 0.05$, or:
$$r^2 + 0.95r - 0.10 = 0 \implies r = \frac{-0.95 + \sqrt{0.95^2 + 0.40}}{2} \approx 0.0956 = 9.56\%$$
Since $\text{PV}(r)$ decreases with $r$, the project has positive NPV for $0.05 < r < 9.56\%$: profitable at $r = 8\%$, not profitable at $r = 10\%$. **C** is correct.
questions.pitfall: Ignoring the $(1+r)$ factor gives $r - 0.05 = 0.05 \implies r = 10\%$, falsely making $r=10\%$ look break-even.

questions.title: Spring 2019 MC · Problem 1
questions.promptMarkdown: The present value of $40$ million paid $7$ years from now with $12\%$ interest and annual compounding is:
rubricChecks: Apply single-payment discounting PV = K / (1 + r)^n
Compute 40 / 1.12^7 ≈ 18.09 million
hints: Hint 1: Discount a single cash flow $K$ received in $n$ years using $\text{PV} = \frac{K}{(1+r)^n}$ (Ch. 3).
Hint 2: Substitute $K = 40$, $r = 0.12$, and $n = 7$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Using the present value formula with annual compounding ($r = 0.12$, $n = 7$):
$$\text{PV} = \frac{40}{1.12^7} \approx 18.0939\text{ million}$$
Therefore **B** ($18.09$ million) is correct.
questions.pitfall: Using simple subtraction $40(1 - 7 \cdot 0.12)$ or discounting only $1$ year ($40/1.12 = 35.71$, trap D) misapplies compound discounting.

questions.title: Spring 2019 MC · Problem 2
questions.promptMarkdown:
Which differentiation is **not** correct?

- **(A)** If $f(x) = x^2 e^x$ then $f'(x) = x(x+2)e^x$
- **(B)** If $f(x) = \dfrac{\ln(x)}{x^2}$ then $f'(x) = \dfrac{1 - 2\ln(x)}{x^3}$
- **(C)** If $f(x) = \sqrt{x^2+1}$ then $f'(x) = \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}$
- **(D)** If $f(x) = \dfrac{x-1}{x+2}$ then $f'(x) = \dfrac{1}{(x+2)^2}$
rubricChecks: Verify product, quotient, and chain rules across candidates A-D
hints: Hint 1: Check each candidate systematically with the product rule, quotient rule $\left(\frac{u}{v}\right)' = \frac{u'v - uv'}{v^2}$, and chain rule (Ch. 11).
Hint 2: Apply the quotient rule carefully to $f(x) = \frac{x-1}{x+2}$ — watch the minus sign on $-(x-1)$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
- **(A)** Product rule: $(x^2)'e^x + x^2(e^x)' = 2xe^x + x^2e^x = x(x+2)e^x$ (correct).
- **(B)** Quotient rule: $\frac{\frac{1}{x}x^2 - \ln(x)\cdot 2x}{x^4} = \frac{1 - 2\ln(x)}{x^3}$ (correct).
- **(C)** Chain rule: $\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x^2+1}} \cdot 2x = \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}$ (correct).
- **(D)** Quotient rule: $\frac{1\cdot(x+2) - (x-1)\cdot 1}{(x+2)^2} = \frac{3}{(x+2)^2} \ne \frac{1}{(x+2)^2}$ (**not** correct).

Hence **D** is the incorrect differentiation.
questions.pitfall: Writing $x + 2 - x - 1 = 1$ instead of $(x + 2) - (x - 1) = 3$ in the quotient rule numerator is a classic sign error.

questions.title: Spring 2019 MC · Problem 3
questions.promptMarkdown: We have the function $f(x) = e^{-x}$. What is correct?
options: The graph of $f(x)$ does not intersect the $y$-axis
rubricChecks: Recall e^u > 0 for all real u, so e^{-x} > 0 everywhere
Confirm f(0) = 1 (y-intercept exists) and f'(x) = -e^{-x} < 0 (decreasing)
hints: Hint 1: Recall the domain, range, and monotonicity of $e^{kx}$ across all real $x$ (Ch. 10).
Hint 2: Note $f(x) = e^{-x} = \frac{1}{e^x}$. Can an exponential ever be zero or negative?
questions.solutionMarkdown: Since $e^x > 0$ for every real $x$, $f(x) = e^{-x} = \frac{1}{e^x} > 0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$. Thus $f(x) < 0$ has no solutions (**A** is correct). Also $f(0) = e^0 = 1$ (defined, intersects the $y$-axis at $(0,1)$) and $f'(x) = -e^{-x} < 0$ (strictly decreasing).
questions.pitfall: Confusing a negative exponent $e^{-x}$ with a negative function value $-e^x$.

questions.title: Spring 2019 MC · Problem 4
questions.promptMarkdown: Suppose $40$ million is invested today and $70$ million is repaid after $6$ years. Then the internal rate of return of the investment (with annual compounding) is:
rubricChecks: Solve r = (7/4)^(1/6) - 1 ≈ 0.09776 (9.78%) and distinguish rate r from growth factor 1 + r
hints: Hint 1: Set present value of inflow equal to initial outlay: $40(1+r)^6 = 70$ (Ch. 2–3).
Hint 2: Solve $1+r = (70/40)^{1/6}$ and watch whether each option states the interest rate $r$ (decimal or $\%$) vs growth factor $1+r$!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Setting $\text{NPV} = -40 + \frac{70}{(1+r)^6} = 0$ gives $40(1+r)^6 = 70$, so:
$$r = \left(\frac{7}{4}\right)^{1/6} - 1 \approx 1.097757 - 1 = 0.09776 \;(9.78\%)$$
Expressed as a decimal number, $0.097 < r < 0.098$, so **C** is correct (whereas $1.09776$ in D is the growth factor $1+r$, not the IRR $r$).
questions.pitfall: Picking $1.097..1.098$ (option D) confuses the annual growth factor $1+r$ with the internal rate of return $r$.

questions.title: Spring 2019 MC · Problem 5
questions.promptMarkdown: We have the hyperbola function $f(x) = \dfrac{4x - 38}{x - 10}$. Which of the graphs in Figure 1 is the graph of $f(x)$?
rubricChecks: Find vertical asymptote x = 10 and horizontal asymptote y = 4
Check y-intercept f(0) = 3.8 (or f(x) = 4 + 2/(x - 10)) to separate A from C
hints: Hint 1: Determine the vertical asymptote ($x - 10 = 0$) and horizontal asymptote ($\lim_{x\to\pm\infty} f(x)$) first (Ch. 9).
Hint 2: Rewrite $f(x) = \frac{4(x-10)+2}{x-10} = 4 + \frac{2}{x-10}$ (or evaluate $f(9.5)$ and $f(0) = 3.8$) to distinguish the two curves sharing $x=10, y=4$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
By polynomial division (or algebraic splitting):
$$f(x) = \frac{4(x-10) + 2}{x - 10} = 4 + \frac{2}{x - 10}$$
- Vertical asymptote: $x = 10$ (eliminates B at $x=2$ and D).
- Horizontal asymptote: $y = 4$.
- Check a point or zero: $f(9.5) = 0$ ($x$-intercept at $9.5$, just left of $x=10$), while graph C crosses the $x$-axis near $x=8.5$. Thus $f(x)$ is **graph A (green)**.
questions.pitfall: Stopping after finding the asymptotes $x=10$ and $y=4$ leaves both green (A) and blue (C) viable; always verify one intercept or test point.

questions.title: Spring 2019 MC · Problem 6
questions.promptMarkdown: Figure 2 shows an ellipse. Which equation defines the ellipse?
rubricChecks: Read centre (x0, y0) = (1, 2) from extreme points x in [-3, 5] and y in [-1, 5]
Identify horizontal semi-axis a = 4 and vertical semi-axis b = 3 and convert standard form to 9(x-1)^2 + 16(y-2)^2 = 144
hints: Hint 1: Read the bounding box of the ellipse from the grid ($x \in [-3, 5]$, $y \in [-1, 5]$) to find the centre $(x_0, y_0)$ and semi-axes $a, b$ (Ch. 8).
Hint 2: Write $\frac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} + \frac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2} = 1$ and multiply both sides by $144 = 16 \cdot 9$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
From Figure 2, the ellipse spans $x \in [-3, 5]$ and $y \in [-1, 5]$:
- Centre: $(x_0, y_0) = \left(\frac{-3+5}{2}, \frac{-1+5}{2}\right) = (1, 2)$.
- Horizontal semi-axis: $a = 5 - 1 = 4 \implies a^2 = 16$.
- Vertical semi-axis: $b = 5 - 2 = 3 \implies b^2 = 9$.

In standard form:
$$\frac{(x-1)^2}{16} + \frac{(y-2)^2}{9} = 1$$
Multiplying both sides by $144$ yields $9(x-1)^2 + 16(y-2)^2 = 144$, so **A** is correct.
questions.pitfall: Swapping $a^2$ and $b^2$ when clearing denominators leads to option C (which is taller than wide).

questions.title: Spring 2019 MC · Problem 7
questions.promptMarkdown: The equation $x - 9\sqrt{x} - 22 = 0$ has:
rubricChecks: Substitute u = sqrt(x) >= 0 to form u^2 - 9u - 22 = 0
Reject u = -2 < 0 and keep u = 11 => x = 121 (one valid solution)
hints: Hint 1: Substitute $u = \sqrt{x}$ (remembering the domain/range condition $u \ge 0$) to turn the equation into a quadratic in $u$ (Ch. 5 & 7).
Hint 2: Factor $u^2 - 9u - 22 = 0$ and check how many roots satisfy $\sqrt{x} \ge 0$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Let $u = \sqrt{x} \ge 0$ (with $x \ge 0$). Since $x = u^2$, the equation becomes:
$$u^2 - 9u - 22 = 0 \implies (u - 11)(u + 2) = 0$$
The roots in $u$ are $u = 11$ and $u = -2$. Because $\sqrt{x} \ge 0$ by definition, $u = -2$ is impossible, leaving only $u = 11 \implies x = 121$. Thus the equation has **a solution** (one solution, **B**).
questions.pitfall: Squaring $u = -2$ blindly to get $x = 4$ gives an extraneous root ($4 - 9\sqrt{4} - 22 = -36 \ne 0$) and trap C.

hints: Hint 1: Interpret the powers via compounding frequency at a fixed nominal rate (Ch. 2 & 4): for a fixed nominal rate $r > 0$, more frequent compounding always yields a strictly larger effective growth factor, with continuous compounding $e^r$ as the upper limit.
Hint 2: Take the $100\,000$-th root of options B–D to compare $1.12$ (annual), $1.04^3$ ($3$ times/year at $12\%$ nominal), and $e^{0.12}$ (continuous at $12\%$ nominal).

Compare annual growth factors for a given nominal interest rate:

Since $1.12 < 1.04^3 < e^{0.12}$, raising to the positive power $100\,000$ gives:
$$1.12^{100\,000} < 1.04^{300\,000} < e^{12\,000}$$
Thus **D** is true.
questions.pitfall: Trying to punch $1.04^{300\,000}$ directly into a calculator causes numeric overflow; always reduce to a 1-year base first.

questions.title: Spring 2019 MC · Problem 9
questions.promptMarkdown: The inequality $\dfrac{(x-1)(12-3x)}{x-2} \le 0$ has the solutions:
rubricChecks: Identify critical points x = 1, x = 4 (zeros) and x = 2 (undefined pole)
Build sign diagram watching the negative coefficient in (12 - 3x) = -3(x - 4) and exclude x = 2
hints: Hint 1: The expression is already factored with $0$ on the right-hand side. Find the zeros of each factor ($x=1$, $x=4$, $x=2$) and build a sign chart (Ch. 7).
Hint 2: Watch two traps: $(12 - 3x)$ is positive for $x < 4$ and negative for $x > 4$, and $x = 2$ makes the denominator zero so it can never be included!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Critical points are $x = 1$ (zero), $x = 2$ (denominator zero, excluded), and $12 - 3x = 0 \iff x = 4$ (zero). Sign analysis of $\frac{(x-1)(12-3x)}{x-2}$:
- $x < 1$: $\frac{(-)(+)}{(-)} = + > 0$
- $1 < x < 2$: $\frac{(+)(+)}{(-)} = - < 0$
- $2 < x < 4$: $\frac{(+)(+)}{(+)} = + > 0$
- $x > 4$: $\frac{(+)(-)}{(+)} = - < 0$

Including the numerator zeros $x=1, 4$ and excluding $x=2$ gives $x \in [1, 2\rangle \cup [4, \infty\rangle$, so **C** is correct.
questions.pitfall: Treating $(12 - 3x)$ like $(x - 4)$ reverses every sign in the sign chart.

questions.title: Spring 2019 MC · Problem 11
questions.promptMarkdown: Let $p$ be the price of a commodity and suppose $D(p) = 100 - 2p$ for $0 < p < 50$ is the demand function. Which statement is true?
options: If $0 < p < 25$ the demand is elastic
If $p = 20$ the demand is unit elastic
If $25 < p < 50$ the demand is elastic
If $10 < p < 40$ the demand is inelastic
rubricChecks: Write price elasticity epsilon(p) = D'(p)*p / D(p) = -2p / (100 - 2p)
Solve epsilon(p) < -1 on 0 < p < 50 to obtain 25 < p < 50
hints: Hint 1: Use the price elasticity formula $\varepsilon(p) = \frac{D'(p) \cdot p}{D(p)}$; demand is elastic when $\varepsilon(p) < -1$ (Ch. 17).
Hint 2: Substitute $D'(p) = -2$ and solve $\frac{-2p}{100 - 2p} < -1$ noting $100 - 2p > 0$ for $0 < p < 50$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
The price elasticity of demand is:
$$\varepsilon(p) = \frac{D'(p) \cdot p}{D(p)} = \frac{-2p}{100 - 2p}$$
Demand is elastic when $\varepsilon(p) < -1$. Since $100 - 2p > 0$ for $0 < p < 50$, we can multiply by $100 - 2p$:
$$-2p < -(100 - 2p) \iff -4p < -100 \iff p > 25$$
Hence demand is elastic for $25 < p < 50$ (unit elastic at $p=25$, inelastic for $0 < p < 25$). **C** is correct.
questions.pitfall: Reversing elastic ($\varepsilon < -1$, high price on linear demand) vs inelastic ($-1 < \varepsilon < 0$, low price).

questions.title: Spring 2019 MC · Problem 12
questions.promptMarkdown: Which of these functions has no vertical asymptote?
rubricChecks: Check domain boundaries and denominator zeros for all four functions
Complete the square x^2 - 6x + 10 = (x - 3)^2 + 1 >= 1 > 0 to show denominator never vanishes

Hint 2: Check the discriminant (or complete the square) of $x^2 - 6x + 10$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
- **(A)** $\lim_{x \to 0^+} \ln(x) = -\infty$, so $x = 0$ is a one-sided vertical asymptote.
- **(B)** $x^2 + 6x + 5 = (x+1)(x+5) = 0$ gives vertical asymptotes $x = -1$ and $x = -5$.
- **(C)** $2x + 5 = 0$ gives vertical asymptote $x = -2.5$.
- **(D)** Completing the square gives $x^2 - 6x + 10 = (x-3)^2 + 1 \ge 1 > 0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$. Since the denominator is never $0$ and $e^x$ is continuous everywhere, $f(x)$ has **no vertical asymptote** (**D**).
questions.pitfall: Forgetting that $\ln(x)$ has a vertical asymptote at $x = 0$ and picking A without checking D.

questions.title: Spring 2019 MC · Problem 13
questions.promptMarkdown: In Figure 3 we see the graph of the **second derivative** $f''(x)$. Which statement is true?
options: $f(x)$ has to be decreasing for $x$ between $2$ and $3$
rubricChecks: Read the plotted curve as f''(x), NOT f(x) or f'(x)
Recognise that f'(x) is concave when (f')'' = f'''(x) <= 0, i.e. when the slope of the plotted f''(x) graph is negative (true on [7, 10])
hints: Hint 1: Read the axis label carefully: the curve shown is $g(x) = f''(x)$! Remember that any function $h(x)$ is concave where $h''(x) \le 0$, i.e. where $h'(x)$ is decreasing (Ch. 14).
Hint 2: For $h(x) = f'(x)$, its first derivative is $h'(x) = f''(x)$ (the plotted curve!). On $[7, 10]$, is the plotted curve $f''(x)$ increasing or decreasing?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Check each option carefully against the graph of $f''(x)$:
- **(A)** On $[5, 8]$, $f''(x) \ge 0$, so $f(x)$ is **convex**, not concave.
- **(B)** A function $h(x) = f'(x)$ is concave where $h''(x) = (f'(x))'' = f'''(x) \le 0$, which means the slope of the $f''(x)$ graph is negative ($f''(x)$ is decreasing). From Figure 3, $f''(x)$ decreases from its peak near $x=6.5$ down to its trough near $x=10.3$, so throughout $[7, 10]$ we have $f'''(x) \le 0$ and $f'(x)$ is concave (**B** is true).
- **(C)** On $[2, 5]$, $f''(x) \le 0$, so $f'(x)$ is decreasing and $f'(2) > f'(5)$.
- **(D)** Knowing $f''(x) < 0$ on $[2, 3]$ tells us $f'(x)$ decreases, not that $f'(x) < 0$ (adding $1000x$ to $f(x)$ leaves $f''(x)$ unchanged while making $f$ increasing).
questions.pitfall: Confusing concavity of $f(x)$ (sign of $f''$) with concavity of $f'(x)$ (slope of $f''$, i.e. sign of $f'''$).

questions.title: Spring 2019 MC · Problem 14
questions.promptMarkdown: We want to write all third degree polynomials of the form $x^3 + bx^2 + cx + d$ which have three zeros; the middle one of the zeros should be $3$ more than the smallest and $4$ less than the largest. Which of these polynomials is **not** such a polynomial?
rubricChecks: Solve each linear factor = 0 to list the three roots in ascending order
Check spacing (middle - smallest = 3 and largest - middle = 4); show option B has spacing 4 then 3
hints: Hint 1: Be careful with signs! A factor $(x - t + 3)$ vanishes at $x = t - 3$, NOT $t + 3$ (Ch. 6).
Hint 2: List the three roots of each option in increasing order and compute the two gaps (must be $+3$, then $+4$).
questions.solutionMarkdown:
List the three zeros in ascending order and check the gaps (required: $+3$, then $+4$):
- **(A)** Zeros: $r - 3 < r < r + 4$ (gaps $3$ and $4$ — valid).
- **(B)** Zeros: $t - 7 < t - 3 < t$ (gaps $(t-3)-(t-7) = 4$ and $t - (t-3) = 3$ — **reversed**, invalid!).
- **(C)** Zeros: $k < k + 3 < k + 7$ (gaps $3$ and $4$ — valid).
- **(D)** Zeros: $s - 1 < s + 2 < s + 6$ (gaps $3$ and $4$ — valid).

Thus **B** is not such a polynomial.
questions.pitfall: Reading the constants $+3, +7$ inside $(x - t + 3)(x - t + 7)$ as roots $t+3, t+7$ instead of solving $x - t + 3 = 0 \implies x = t - 3$.

questions.title: Spring 2019 MC · Problem 15
questions.promptMarkdown: We have the function expression $f(x) = \dfrac{5x - 3}{x - 1}$ with domain of definition $D_f = \langle 1, \infty\rangle$. Which statement is true?
options: $f(x)$ has an inverse function $g(x)$ with domain of definition $D_g = \langle -\infty, 5\rangle \cup \langle 5, \infty\rangle$
$f(x)$ has an inverse function $g(x)$ with domain of definition $D_g = \langle -\infty, 5\rangle$
$f(x)$ has an inverse function $g(x)$ with domain of definition $D_g = \langle 5, \infty\rangle$
rubricChecks: Show f(x) = 5 + 2/(x - 1) (or f'(x) = -2/(x - 1)^2 < 0) so f is strictly decreasing on <1, inf> and invertible
Determine D_g = R_f using limits as x -> 1+ (+inf) and x -> +inf (5+), giving D_g = <5, inf>
hints: Hint 1: Check monotonicity of $f(x)$ on $\langle 1, \infty\rangle$, and recall that the domain of the inverse function is the **range** of $f$ on its restricted domain: $D_g = R_f$ (Ch. 10).
Hint 2: Rewrite $f(x) = 5 + \frac{2}{x-1}$ and evaluate $\lim_{x \to 1^+} f(x)$ and $\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x)$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Rewrite $f(x) = \frac{5(x-1)+2}{x-1} = 5 + \frac{2}{x-1}$. Since $f'(x) = -\frac{2}{(x-1)^2} < 0$ for all $x > 1$, $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing on $D_f = \langle 1, \infty\rangle$ and therefore has an inverse function $g(x)$.

The domain of $g$ equals the range of $f$ on $\langle 1, \infty\rangle$:
$$\lim_{x \to 1^+} \left(5 + \frac{2}{x-1}\right) = \infty, \qquad \lim_{x \to \infty} \left(5 + \frac{2}{x-1}\right) = 5^+$$
By continuity, $D_g = R_f = \langle 5, \infty\rangle$, so **D** is correct.
questions.pitfall: Determining $D_g$ by looking at the algebraic formula $g(x) = \frac{x-3}{x-5}$ alone gives $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{5\}$ (trap B), ignoring that $D_f$ was restricted to $x > 1$.

questions.promptMarkdown: We have a function $f(x)$ with the graph in Figure 1. Which statement is **not** correct?

hints: Hint 1: A parabola with vertex $(x_0, y_0) = (4, 1)$ has vertex form $f(x) = a(x - 4)^2 + 1$ with $a > 0$ (Ch. 8).
Hint 2: Substitute $f(2) = 3$ to find $a$, then expand $(x - 4)^2$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Using vertex form with minimum at $(4, 1)$:
$$f(x) = a(x - 4)^2 + 1$$
Substitute $f(2) = 3$: $a(2 - 4)^2 + 1 = 3 \implies 4a = 2 \implies a = \frac{1}{2} > 0$. Expanding:
$$f(x) = \frac{1}{2}(x^2 - 8x + 16) + 1 = \frac{1}{2}x^2 - 4x + 9$$
Hence **C** is correct.
questions.pitfall: Assuming $a = 1$ without checking $f(2) = 3$ selects trap B ($f(2) = 5 \ne 3$).

questions.title: Autumn 2018 MC · Problem 5
questions.promptMarkdown: A fixed amount $90\,000$ (the annuity) is to be paid annually for $20$ years with the first payment three years from now. Suppose the interest is $4\%$ with annual compounding. Then the geometric series which gives the present value of this cash flow is:
rubricChecks: Discount the first payment at t = 3 by 1.04^3
Count 20 annual terms accurately: exponents 3, 4, ..., 3 + 20 - 1 = 22
hints: Hint 1: Count the exponents carefully! An integer range from $m$ to $M$ inclusive contains $M - m + 1$ terms (Ch. 4).
Hint 2: Starting at $t = 3$, what exponent gives the $20$-th payment ($3 + 19$)?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
The first payment is at $t = 3$, giving first term $\frac{90\,000}{1.04^3}$. Since there are $20$ annual payments in total, the $k$-th payment occurs at $t = 2 + k$, so the $20$-th payment occurs at $t = 2 + 20 = 22$ ($22 - 3 + 1 = 20$ terms):
$$\frac{90\,000}{1.04^3} + \frac{90\,000}{1.04^4} + \cdots + \frac{90\,000}{1.04^{21}} + \frac{90\,000}{1.04^{22}}$$
Hence **B** is correct.
questions.pitfall: Fencepost error: adding $3 + 20 = 23$ (option A) gives $23 - 3 + 1 = 21$ payments instead of $20$.

questions.title: Autumn 2018 MC · Problem 6
questions.promptMarkdown: The equation $\sqrt{2x + 3} = x + 4$ has:
rubricChecks: Square both sides to obtain x^2 + 6x + 13 = 0
Complete the square (x + 3)^2 = -4 (or discriminant 36 - 52 = -16 < 0) to conclude zero real solutions
hints: Hint 1: Square both sides of $\sqrt{2x+3} = x + 4$ and bring all terms to one side (Ch. 5 & 7).
Hint 2: Check the discriminant $b^2 - 4ac$ (or complete the square) of $x^2 + 6x + 13 = 0$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Squaring both sides yields:
$$2x + 3 = (x + 4)^2 = x^2 + 8x + 16 \implies x^2 + 6x + 13 = 0$$
Completing the square gives $(x + 3)^2 + 4 = 0$, i.e. $(x + 3)^2 = -4$, which has no real solutions (discriminant $\Delta = 6^2 - 4 \cdot 13 = -16 < 0$). Thus the original equation has **no solutions** (**A**).
questions.pitfall: Making an expansion mistake $(x+4)^2 = x^2 + 16$ instead of $x^2 + 8x + 16$.

questions.title: Autumn 2018 MC · Problem 7
questions.promptMarkdown: Hege deposits $300\,000$ into an account earning $2.4\%$ interest and with continuous compounding. How long time will it take before the balance is $500\,000$?
rubricChecks: Set up continuous compounding equation 300000 * e^{0.024t} = 500000
Take natural logarithms: 0.024t = ln(5/3) = ln 5 - ln 3 => t = (ln 5 - ln 3)/0.024
hints: Hint 1: Under continuous compounding at nominal rate $r$, capital grows as $K(t) = K_0 e^{rt}$ (Ch. 4 & 10).
Hint 2: Divide by $300\,000$ to get $e^{0.024t} = \frac{5}{3}$ and apply $\ln$ using $\ln(5/3) = \ln 5 - \ln 3$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
With continuous compounding at $r = 0.024$, the balance after $t$ years is $300\,000 e^{0.024t} = 500\,000$:
$$e^{0.024t} = \frac{5}{3} \implies 0.024t = \ln\!\left(\frac{5}{3}\right) = \ln 5 - \ln 3$$
Hence $t = \dfrac{\ln 5 - \ln 3}{0.024} \approx 21.28$ years (**A**).
questions.pitfall: Using annual compounding $300\,000 \cdot 1.024^t = 500\,000$ yields option C ($\frac{\ln 5 - \ln 3}{\ln(1.024)}$) instead of continuous compounding.

questions.title: Autumn 2018 MC · Problem 8
questions.promptMarkdown: We have a cost function $K(x) = 0.01x^2 + 15x + 1600$. Then the minimal average unit cost is:
rubricChecks: Form average unit cost A(x) = K(x)/x = 0.01x + 15 + 1600/x and solve A'(x) = 0 (or K'(x) = A(x))
Find cost optimum quantity x = 400 and evaluate minimal unit cost A(400) = 23
hints: Hint 1: Cost optimum occurs where marginal cost equals average unit cost: $K'(x) = A(x) = \frac{K(x)}{x}$ (or $A'(x) = 0$, Ch. 16).
Hint 2: Note the question asks for the **minimal average unit cost** $A(x^*)$, NOT the optimal quantity $x^*$!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Average unit cost is $A(x) = \frac{K(x)}{x} = 0.01x + 15 + \frac{1600}{x}$ and marginal cost is $K'(x) = 0.02x + 15$ (with $K''(x) = 0.02 > 0$). Setting $K'(x) = A(x)$:
$$0.02x + 15 = 0.01x + 15 + \frac{1600}{x} \implies 0.01x = \frac{1600}{x} \implies x^2 = 160\,000 \implies x = 400$$
Evaluating the minimal average unit cost at $x = 400$:
$$A(400) = K'(400) = 0.02 \cdot 400 + 15 = 8 + 15 = 23$$
Thus **B** ($23$) is correct.
questions.pitfall: Stopping at the optimal quantity $x = 400$ (trap A) or total cost $K(400) = 9200$ (trap D) instead of evaluating $A(400) = 23$.

questions.title: Autumn 2018 MC · Problem 9
questions.promptMarkdown: We have the function $f(x) = 3\ln(x) - 0.5x + 10,\; x > 0$. Which statement is **not** correct?
options: $f(x)$ has a global maximum point for $x = 6$
rubricChecks: Compute f'(x) = 3/x - 0.5 = (3 - 0.5x)/x and verify global max at x = 6
hints: Hint 1: Differentiate $f(x)$ once and twice for $x > 0$: $(\ln x)' = x^{-1}$ and $(x^{-1})' = -x^{-2}$ (Ch. 11, 12 & 14).
Hint 2: Check the sign of $f''(3)$ carefully.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
For $x > 0$, we compute:
$$f'(x) = \frac{3}{x} - 0.5 = \frac{3 - 0.5x}{x}, \qquad f''(x) = -\frac{3}{x^2}$$
- $f'(x) > 0$ on $\langle 0, 6\rangle$ and $f'(x) < 0$ on $\langle 6, \infty\rangle$, so (A), (B), and (C) are all true.
- At $x = 3$, $f''(3) = -\frac{3}{3^2} = -\frac{1}{3} \ne \frac{1}{3}$, so **(D)** is **not** correct.
questions.pitfall: Dropping the minus sign when differentiating $3x^{-1} \to -3x^{-2}$.

questions.title: Autumn 2018 MC · Problem 10
questions.promptMarkdown: Let $p$ be the price of a commodity and suppose $D(p) = 75e^{-0.2p}$ is the demand function. Which statement is correct?
options: If $p = 10$ the demand is unit elastic
rubricChecks: Compute D'(p) = -15e^{-0.2p} and simplify epsilon(p) = D'(p)*p / D(p) = -0.2p
Solve epsilon(p) < -1 => -0.2p < -1 => p > 5 for elastic demand
hints: Hint 1: Compute $\varepsilon(p) = \frac{D'(p) \cdot p}{D(p)}$; notice the exponential factor $75e^{-0.2p}$ cancels cleanly (Ch. 17).
Hint 2: Demand is elastic when $\varepsilon(p) < -1$, i.e. $-0.2p < -1$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Since $D'(p) = 75(-0.2)e^{-0.2p} = -15e^{-0.2p}$, the price elasticity simplifies to:
$$\varepsilon(p) = \frac{D'(p) \cdot p}{D(p)} = \frac{-15e^{-0.2p} \cdot p}{75e^{-0.2p}} = -0.2p$$
Demand is elastic when $\varepsilon(p) < -1 \iff -0.2p < -1 \iff p > 5$ (and unit elastic at $p = 5$). Thus **C** is correct.
questions.pitfall: Dividing by $-0.2$ without flipping the inequality sign gives $p < 5$ (trap B).

questions.title: Autumn 2018 MC · Problem 11
questions.promptMarkdown: We have $a = \lim_{x \to 1} \dfrac{e^x - e}{x - \sqrt{x}}$. Which statement is correct?
rubricChecks: Verify 0/0 indeterminate form at x = 1
Apply L'Hôpital's rule with (e^x - e)' = e^x and (x - sqrt(x))' = 1 - 1/(2*sqrt(x)) to get e / (1/2) = 2e
hints: Hint 1: Check that substituting $x = 1$ gives $\frac{0}{0}$, so L'Hôpital's rule applies (Ch. 15).
Hint 2: Differentiate numerator and denominator separately: remember $e$ is a constant ($(e)' = 0$) and $(\sqrt{x})' = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
As $x \to 1$, both $e^x - e \to 0$ and $x - \sqrt{x} \to 0$ ($\frac{0}{0}$ form). Applying L'Hôpital's rule:
$$a = \lim_{x \to 1} \frac{e^x - e}{x - \sqrt{x}} = \lim_{x \to 1} \frac{e^x}{1 - \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}} = \frac{e}{1 - \frac{1}{2}} = \frac{e}{\frac{1}{2}} = 2e$$
Hence **B** ($a = 2e$) is correct.
questions.pitfall: Dividing $e$ by $1/2$ as $e/2$ (trap C) or differentiating the constant $e$ as $e$ instead of $0$.

questions.title: Autumn 2018 MC · Problem 12
questions.promptMarkdown: We have a function $f(x)$ with **derivative function** $f'(x)$ which has the graph in Figure 2. Which statement is correct?
rubricChecks: Connect convexity of f(x) (f''(x) >= 0) to f'(x) being increasing

hints: Hint 1: Figure 2 shows $f'(x)$, so $f''(x)$ is the **slope** of the plotted graph! Where is $f''(x) \ge 0$ (Ch. 14)?

questions.solutionMarkdown: Since $f''(x) = (f'(x))'$ is the slope of the plotted graph of $f'(x)$, $f(x)$ is convex wherever $f'(x)$ is increasing. From Figure 2, $f'(x)$ increases throughout $[1, 5]$ (reaching its peak at $x = 5$) and decreases for $x > 5$. Thus $f''(x) \ge 0$ on $[1, 5]$ and $f(x)$ is convex in $[1, 5]$ (**D**).
questions.pitfall: Looking at the bell-shaped curvature of the $f'(x)$ graph near $x=5$ (which is $f''' < 0$) instead of its slope ($f'' \ge 0$ on $[1,5]$) lures students into trap A.

questions.title: Autumn 2018 MC · Problem 14
questions.promptMarkdown: We have a curve implicitly defined by the equation $4x^2 - 7xy + 4y^2 = 16$. Which statement is correct?
options: There is only one point on the curve with $x$-coordinate $4$ and the slope of the tangent at this point is equal to $-1$
There are two points on the curve with $x$-coordinate $4$ and the product of the slopes of the tangents at these points is $-2.75$
There are two points on the curve with $x$-coordinate $4$ and the product of the slopes of the tangents at these points is $-64$
There are two points on the curve with $x$-coordinate $4$ and the product of the slopes of the tangents at these points is $\frac{1024}{425}$
rubricChecks: Substitute x = 4 into 4x^2 - 7xy + 4y^2 = 16 to solve y^2 - 7y + 12 = 0 => (4, 3) and (4, 4)
Differentiate implicitly 8x - 7y - 7xy' + 8yy' = 0 => y' = (7y - 8x)/(8y - 7x)
hints: Hint 1: First substitute $x = 4$ into $4x^2 - 7xy + 4y^2 = 16$ to find all matching $y$-coordinates on the curve (Ch. 5 & 13).
Hint 2: Differentiate $4x^2 - 7xy + 4y^2 = 16$ implicitly with respect to $x$ (use the product rule on $-7xy$!), solve for $y'$, and evaluate at both points.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
1. **Points with $x = 4$:** $4(16) - 28y + 4y^2 = 16 \implies 4y^2 - 28y + 48 = 0 \implies y^2 - 7y + 12 = 0$, giving $y = 3$ and $y = 4$, i.e. two points $(4, 3)$ and $(4, 4)$.
2. **Implicit differentiation:**
$$8x - 7y - 7xy' + 8yy' = 0 \implies (8y - 7x)y' = 7y - 8x \implies y' = \frac{7y - 8x}{8y - 7x}$$
3. **Slopes & product:**
   - At $(4, 3)$: $y' = \frac{21 - 32}{24 - 28} = \frac{-11}{-4} = \frac{11}{4} = 2.75$.
   - At $(4, 4)$: $y' = \frac{28 - 32}{32 - 28} = \frac{-4}{4} = -1$.

The product of the slopes is $2.75 \cdot (-1) = -2.75$, so **B** is correct.
questions.pitfall: Forgetting the product rule on $-7xy$ (writing $-7y'$ instead of $-7y - 7xy'$) ruins the implicit derivative formula.

questions.title: Autumn 2018 MC · Problem 15
questions.promptMarkdown: We have the function expression $f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x + 4$. Which statement is correct?
options: If the domain of definition $D_f$ is $[4, \infty\rangle$ then $f(x)$ has an inverse function.
If the domain of definition $D_f$ is $[3, \infty\rangle$ then $f(x)$ has no inverse function.
If the domain of definition $D_f$ is $[0, 3]$ then $f(x)$ has an inverse function.
If the domain of definition $D_f$ is $\langle -\infty, 1]$ then $f(x)$ has no inverse function.
rubricChecks: Identify monotone intervals <-inf, 1], [1, 3], [3, inf> and conclude [4, inf> subset [3, inf> is strictly increasing and invertible
hints: Hint 1: A continuous function has an inverse on an interval if and only if it is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing across that entire interval (Ch. 10 & 12).
Hint 2: Solve $f'(x) = 3x^2 - 12x + 9 = 0$ to find the turning points of the cubic.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Differentiate and factor:
$$f'(x) = 3x^2 - 12x + 9 = 3(x^2 - 4x + 3) = 3(x - 1)(x - 3)$$
- $f'(x) > 0$ on $\langle -\infty, 1\rangle$ and $\langle 3, \infty\rangle$, and $f'(x) < 0$ on $\langle 1, 3\rangle$.
- Therefore $f$ is strictly increasing on $\langle -\infty, 1]$ and on $[3, \infty\rangle$ (so B and D are false, while $[0, 3]$ spans the local max at $x=1$ so C is false).
- Since $[4, \infty\rangle \subset [3, \infty\rangle$, $f(x)$ is strictly increasing on $[4, \infty\rangle$ and has an inverse function (**A**).
questions.pitfall: Thinking invertibility requires starting at the exact stationary point $x=3$; any sub-interval $[4, \infty\rangle$ of a strictly monotone region is also strictly monotone.

questions.title: Autumn 2025 Exam · Problem 1
questions.promptMarkdown:
**i)** Use polynomial division to calculate $(x^3 + 11x^2 + 40x + 50) : (x + 5)$ with remainder.

**ii)** Factorise $x^3 + 11x^2 + 40x + 50$.
rubricChecks: Execute polynomial long division to obtain quotient x^2 + 6x + 10 and remainder 0
Check whether x^2 + 6x + 10 has real zeros via completing the square (x + 3)^2 + 1 > 0 or discriminant -4 < 0
State final complete real factorisation (x + 5)(x^2 + 6x + 10)
hints: Hint 1: Set up standard polynomial long division matching leading terms $x^3 / x = x^2$, $6x^2 / x = 6x$, and $10x / x = 10$ (Ch. 6).
Hint 2: Once you have $(x+5)(x^2+6x+10)$, check the discriminant $b^2 - 4ac$ (or complete the square) on $x^2 + 6x + 10$ before stopping.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** Carrying out polynomial long division:
$$(x^3 + 11x^2 + 40x + 50) : (x + 5) = x^2 + 6x + 10$$
with remainder **$0$** (since $x^3+5x^2$ leaves $6x^2+40x$; subtracting $6x^2+30x$ leaves $10x+50$; subtracting $10x+50$ leaves $0$).

**ii)** Completing the square on the quadratic quotient gives $x^2 + 6x + 10 = (x + 3)^2 + 1 \ge 1 > 0$, which has no real zeros. Hence it cannot be factorised further over $\mathbb{R}$, and:
$$x^3 + 11x^2 + 40x + 50 = (x + 5)(x^2 + 6x + 10)$$
questions.pitfall: Failing to prove that $x^2 + 6x + 10$ has no real roots (you must justify irreducibility via discriminant or completing the square for full marks).

questions.title: Autumn 2025 Exam · Problem 2
questions.promptMarkdown:
**i)** Calculate the sum of the geometric series:
$$\frac{20\,000}{1.03^2} + \frac{20\,000}{1.03^3} + \cdots + \frac{20\,000}{1.03^{24}} + \frac{20\,000}{1.03^{25}}$$

**ii)** Describe a financial situation where this sum is relevant (the important numbers should be interpreted).
rubricChecks: Count exact number of terms n = 25 - 2 + 1 = 24
Evaluate the geometric series sum to 328,845.48
Interpret 20,000 (annual payment), 3% (annual interest/discount rate), t = 2 (first payment), and t = 25 (24th/last payment) as present value or loan principal
hints: Hint 1: Read the series backwards with $a_1 = \frac{20\,000}{1.03^{25}}$ and $k = 1.03$, and count exponents from $2$ to $25$ carefully ($25 - 2 + 1$ terms, Ch. 4).
Hint 2: For part (ii), interpret the sum as the **present value today** (e.g. maximum loan principal) of an annual cash flow, explicitly naming $20\,000$, $3\%$, year $2$, and year $25$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** Reading the series from right to left gives first term $a_1 = \frac{20\,000}{1.03^{25}}$, ratio $k = 1.03$, and $n = 25 - 2 + 1 = 24$ terms:
$$S = \frac{20\,000}{1.03^{25}} \cdot \frac{1.03^{24} - 1}{1.03 - 1} = \frac{20\,000}{1.03^{25}} \cdot \frac{1.03^{24} - 1}{0.03} \approx 328\,845.48$$

**ii)** The sum represents the **present value today** ($t=0$) of a regular cash flow of **$20\,000$ paid annually** at **$3\%$ annual interest** (annual compounding), where the **first payment occurs $2$ years from now** and the **last ($24$-th) payment occurs $25$ years from now** — for instance, the loan principal borrowed today that is repaid by those $24$ annual instalments.
questions.pitfall: Examiner report note (avg score 43%): many students miscounted $25 - 2 = 23$ terms instead of $24$, or described future savings instead of present value.

questions.title: Autumn 2025 Exam · Problem 3
questions.promptMarkdown:
In Figure 1 you see the graph of the function $f(x)$. Determine whether each statement is **true** or **false**. Give a short explanation.

**i)** $f'(3) > f'(8)$.

**ii)** $f(x)$ has three stationary points in the interval $[2, 8]$.

**iii)** $f(x)$ has two inflection points in the interval $[2, 10]$.
rubricChecks: Conclude (i) FALSE because f'(3) ≈ 0 (near peak) whereas f'(8) > 0 (approx 0.4, rising)
Conclude (ii) FALSE because f'(a) = 0 occurs only twice on [2, 8] (at x ≈ 3 and x ≈ 5.3; the third peak is at x ≈ 9.4 outside [2, 8])
Conclude (iii) TRUE because curvature switches concave->convex at x ≈ 3.7 and convex->concave at x ≈ 6.8
hints: Hint 1: Check what each derivative measures geometrically on the graph of $f(x)$: $f'(x)$ is tangent slope, stationary points have horizontal tangents $f'(a)=0$, and inflection points are where curvature switches between concave and convex (Ch. 11, 12 & 14).
Hint 2: Pay strict attention to the interval endpoints $[2, 8]$ in (ii) vs $[2, 10]$ in (iii)!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i) FALSE.** $f'(x)$ is the slope of the tangent line. Near the local peak $x = 3$, $f'(3) \approx 0$, whereas at $x = 8$ the graph is rising with slope $f'(8) \approx 0.4 > 0$, so $f'(3) < f'(8)$.

**ii) FALSE.** Stationary points satisfy $f'(a) = 0$ (horizontal tangent). Inside $[2, 8]$ there are only **two** stationary points: $x \approx 3$ (local max) and $x \approx 5.3$ (local min). (The next local max at $x \approx 9.4$ lies outside $[2, 8]$.)

**iii) TRUE.** Inflection points occur where $f''(x)$ changes sign (concavity switches). On $[2, 10]$ this happens twice: at $x \approx 3.7$ (concave $\to$ convex) and at $x \approx 6.8$ (convex $\to$ concave).
questions.pitfall: Counting zeros ($x$-intercepts near $2.4, 4.3, 6.8$) instead of horizontal tangents for stationary points, or missing the $[2, 8]$ boundary cutoff.

questions.title: Autumn 2025 Exam · Problem 4
questions.promptMarkdown: The hyperbola function $f(x)$ has $x = 30$ as vertical asymptote and $y = 50$ as horizontal asymptote. Moreover, $f(33) = 48$. Determine the expression of the hyperbola function.
rubricChecks: Write standard hyperbola form f(x) = c + a/(x - b) with b = 30 and c = 50
Substitute f(33) = 48 => 50 + a/3 = 48 => a = -6 and state f(x) = 50 - 6/(x - 30)
hints: Hint 1: Use the standard form of a hyperbola $f(x) = c + \frac{a}{x - b}$, where $x = b$ is the vertical asymptote and $y = c$ is the horizontal asymptote (Ch. 9).
Hint 2: Substitute $b = 30$, $c = 50$, and $f(33) = 48$ to solve for $a$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
In standard form $f(x) = c + \frac{a}{x - b}$, vertical asymptote $x = 30$ gives $b = 30$ and horizontal asymptote $y = 50$ gives $c = 50$:
$$f(x) = 50 + \frac{a}{x - 30}$$
Using $f(33) = 48$: $50 + \frac{a}{33 - 30} = 48 \implies \frac{a}{3} = -2 \implies a = -6$. Therefore:
$$f(x) = 50 - \frac{6}{x - 30} \quad \left(= \frac{50x - 1506}{x - 30}\right)$$
questions.pitfall: Swapping $b = 30$ and $c = 50$ between horizontal and vertical asymptotes.

questions.title: Autumn 2025 Exam · Problem 5
questions.promptMarkdown:
The graphs of the functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are given in Figure 2.

**i)** Use the figure to solve the inequality $f(x) - g(x) > 0$.

**ii)** Use the figure to solve the inequality $\dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)} \le 0$.
rubricChecks: Read intersection points where f(x) > g(x) to get 2 < x < 4.37 and x > 7.4
Identify zeros of f(x) (x = 2, 4, 7) and zeros/poles of g(x) (x = 2, 5, 8) and construct sign diagram
Exclude all zeros of g(x) (including shared zero x = 2!) to state x < 2, 2 < x <= 4, 5 < x <= 7, and x > 8
hints: Hint 1: Part (i) asks where the red curve $f(x)$ lies strictly above the green curve $g(x)$. Part (ii) compares the **signs** of $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ relative to the $x$-axis using a sign diagram (Ch. 7).
Hint 2: In part (ii), check $x = 2, 5, 8$ where $g(x) = 0$: division by zero is undefined even at $x = 2$ where $f(2) = 0$ as well!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** $f(x) - g(x) > 0 \iff f(x) > g(x)$, where the graph of $f$ lies strictly above $g$. From Figure 2, the intersections are at $x = 2$, $x \approx 4.37$, and $x \approx 7.4$, giving:
$$2 < x < 4.37 \quad \text{or} \quad x > 7.4$$

**ii)** From the $x$-intercepts, $f(x) = 0$ at $x = 2, 4, 7$ and $g(x) = 0$ at $x = 2, 5, 8$ (excluded from the domain of $f/g$). Building a sign diagram:
- $x < 2$: $f < 0, g > 0 \implies f/g < 0$
- $2 < x < 4$: $f > 0, g < 0 \implies f/g < 0$ (and $f(4)/g(4) = 0$)
- $4 < x < 5$: $f < 0, g < 0 \implies f/g > 0$
- $5 < x < 7$: $f < 0, g > 0 \implies f/g < 0$ (and $f(7)/g(7) = 0$)
- $7 < x < 8$: $f > 0, g > 0 \implies f/g > 0$
- $x > 8$: $f > 0, g < 0 \implies f/g < 0$

Solutions: **$x < 2$, $2 < x \le 4$, $5 < x \le 7$, and $x > 8$**.
questions.pitfall: Examiner report trap (avg score 49%): including $x = 2$ (writing $x \le 4$) or $x = 5, 8$ where $g(x) = 0$ makes $\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}$ undefined.

questions.title: Autumn 2025 Exam · Problem 6
questions.promptMarkdown:
**i)** Calculate how much you have to deposit today to have $800\,000$ on the account $12$ years from now if the interest is $4.6\%$.

**ii)** You would like the balance on the account $6$ years from now to be $800\,000$ with the same deposit as in (i). Calculate what the interest has to be.
rubricChecks: Compute initial deposit K0 = 800000 / 1.046^12 ≈ 466,347.63
hints: Hint 2: Notice $(1 + r)^6 = 1.046^{12} = (1.046^2)^6$, so $1 + r = 1.046^2$ cleanly without rounding error!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** With annual growth factor $1.046$ over $12$ years, the required deposit today is:
$$K_0 = \frac{800\,000}{1.046^{12}} \approx 466\,347.63$$

**ii)** Let $r$ be the new annual interest rate. To reach $800\,000$ in $6$ years from the same deposit $K_0 = \frac{800\,000}{1.046^{12}}$:
$$\frac{800\,000}{1.046^{12}} \cdot (1 + r)^6 = 800\,000 \implies (1 + r)^6 = 1.046^{12} \implies 1 + r = 1.046^2 = 1.094116$$
Hence $r = 1.046^2 - 1 \approx 0.0941 = \mathbf{9.41\%}$.

questions.title: Autumn 2025 Exam · Problem 7
questions.promptMarkdown:
An ellipse has centre $(3, 5)$, the horizontal semi-axis is $2$ and the vertical semi-axis is $4$.

**i)** Write up the equation for the ellipse on standard form.

**ii)** Make a drawing of the ellipse.
rubricChecks: Write standard ellipse equation (x - 3)^2 / 4 + (y - 5)^2 / 16 = 1
Plot centre (3, 5) and all four vertices (1, 5), (5, 5), (3, 1), and (3, 9) accurately on labelled axes
hints: Hint 1: Recall standard form $\frac{(x - x_0)^2}{a^2} + \frac{(y - y_0)^2}{b^2} = 1$ with centre $(x_0, y_0)$, horizontal semi-axis $a$, and vertical semi-axis $b$ (Ch. 8).
Hint 2: Mark the four extreme points $(3 \pm 2, 5)$ and $(3, 5 \pm 4)$ before sketching a smooth oval.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** Substituting $(x_0, y_0) = (3, 5)$, $a = 2$ ($a^2 = 4$), and $b = 4$ ($b^2 = 16$) into standard form:
$$\frac{(x - 3)^2}{4} + \frac{(y - 5)^2}{16} = 1$$

**ii)** Plot a coordinate grid showing the centre $(3, 5)$, horizontal vertices $(1, 5)$ and $(5, 5)$, and vertical vertices $(3, 1)$ and $(3, 9)$, connected by a smooth symmetric ellipse.
questions.pitfall: Forgetting to square the semi-axes in the denominators (writing $/2$ and $/4$ instead of $/4$ and $/16$).

questions.title: Autumn 2025 Exam · Problem 8
questions.promptMarkdown:
Make a drawing of the graph of a function $f(x)$ with domain of definition $D_f = [5, 30]$ which satisfies the following three requirements:
1. $f(20) = 100$.
2. $f'(x)$ is negative for all $x$.
3. $f''(x) > 0$ for $x < 15$ and $f''(x) < 0$ for $x > 15$.
rubricChecks: Restrict the drawn curve strictly to x in [5, 30] and pass clearly through (20, 100)
Ensure the curve is strictly decreasing across the entire interval [5, 30]
Draw convex curvature (bends upwards) on [5, 15) switching smoothly at inflection point x = 15 to concave curvature (bends downwards) on (15, 30]
hints: Hint 1: Translate the derivative signs into geometry: $f'(x) < 0$ means strictly decreasing everywhere; $f''(x) > 0$ means convex (slope becomes less steep); $f''(x) < 0$ means concave (slope becomes steeper, Ch. 14).

Hint 2: Mark endpoints at $x = 5$ and $x = 30$ only (do not extend past them!), plot $(20, 100)$, and make $x = 15$ a smooth decreasing inflection point without letting the tangent go horizontal if $f'(15) < 0$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
A valid sketch on labelled axes must satisfy all four visual features:
1. **Domain:** Starts at $x = 5$ and ends at $x = 30$ ($D_f = [5, 30]$).
2. **Anchor point:** Passes through $(20, 100)$.
3. **Monotonicity:** Strictly decreasing ($f'(x) < 0$) everywhere, including a negative slope through $x = 15$.
4. **Curvature:** Convex (cupping upwards while falling) on $[5, 15\rangle$, inflection point at $x = 15$, and concave (arching downwards while falling) on $\langle 15, 30]$.
questions.pitfall: Drawing a horizontal tangent at $x = 15$ (which makes $f'(15) = 0$, violating condition 2 that $f'(x)$ is negative for all $x$) or ignoring the domain $[5, 30]$.

questions.title: Autumn 2025 Exam · Problem 9
questions.promptMarkdown:
Let $p$ be the price of a commodity and suppose $D(p) = 150e^{-0.01p^2}$ with $p \ge 0$ is the demand function. Suppose $\varepsilon(p)$ is the momentary price elasticity of the demand function.

**i)** Calculate $\varepsilon(p)$.

**ii)** Determine the price $p$ such that the demand is elastic.

**iii)** Determine whether the revenue is increasing or decreasing if the price increases a little from $p = 10$.
rubricChecks: Apply chain rule D'(p) = 150(-0.02p)e^{-0.01p^2} and simplify epsilon(p) = -0.02p^2
Solve -0.02p^2 < -1 with p >= 0 to obtain p > sqrt(50) (≈ 7.07)
Check p = 10 > sqrt(50) (or epsilon(10) = -2 < -1) and conclude revenue decreases when price increases from 10
hints: Hint 1: Differentiate $D(p) = 150e^{-0.01p^2}$ using the chain rule with inner function $u(p) = -0.01p^2$, then substitute into $\varepsilon(p) = \frac{D'(p) \cdot p}{D(p)}$ (Ch. 17).
Hint 2: Demand is elastic when $\varepsilon(p) < -1$. Remember $R'(p) = D(p)(1 + \varepsilon(p))$: when demand is elastic, raising price lowers revenue!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** By the chain rule, $D'(p) = 150(-0.02p)e^{-0.01p^2}$. Hence:
$$\varepsilon(p) = \frac{D'(p) \cdot p}{D(p)} = \frac{(-0.02p) \cdot 150e^{-0.01p^2} \cdot p}{150e^{-0.01p^2}} = -0.02p^2$$

**ii)** Demand is elastic when $\varepsilon(p) < -1$:
$$-0.02p^2 < -1 \iff p^2 > 50$$
Since $p \ge 0$, demand is elastic for **$p > \sqrt{50}$** ($p > 5\sqrt{2} \approx 7.07$).

**iii)** Since $10 > \sqrt{50}$ (equivalently $\varepsilon(10) = -2 < -1$), demand is price elastic at $p = 10$, so **revenue decreases** if the price increases slightly from $10$.
questions.pitfall: Forgetting the extra factor of $p$ in $\varepsilon(p) = \frac{D'(p) \cdot p}{D(p)}$ gives $-0.02p$ instead of $-0.02p^2$.

questions.title: Autumn 2025 Exam · Problem 10
questions.promptMarkdown: A curve is implicitly defined by the equation $e^y = xy + 2025$ (see Figure 3). Use implicit differentiation to express $y'$ in terms of $y$ and $x$.
rubricChecks: Apply chain rule on LHS: (e^y)' = e^y * y'
Apply product rule on RHS: (xy + 2025)' = y + x*y'
Collect y' terms and isolate y' = y / (e^y - x)
hints: Hint 1: Treat $y = y(x)$ as a function of $x$ and differentiate both sides with respect to $x$: use the chain rule on $e^y$ and the product rule on $xy$ (Ch. 13).
Hint 2: Move all terms containing $y'$ to the left-hand side: $e^y y' - xy' = y$, then factor out $y'$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Differentiating both sides of $e^y = xy + 2025$ with respect to $x$ (chain rule on $e^y$, product rule on $xy$, and $(2025)' = 0$):
$$e^y y' = y + xy'$$
Collecting the $y'$ terms on the left:
$$(e^y - x)y' = y \implies y' = \frac{y}{e^y - x}$$
questions.pitfall: Examiner report note (avg score 37%): writing $(e^y)' = e^y$ (missing $y'$) or $(xy)' = xy'$ (missing $+y$ from the product rule).

questions.title: Autumn 2025 Exam · Problem 11
questions.promptMarkdown:
We have the function
$$f(x) = \ln\!\left(\frac{50e^{0.03x} + 1}{120e^{0.03x} + 2025}\right)$$
Determine possible horizontal and vertical asymptotes of $f(x)$.
rubricChecks: Evaluate limit as x -> -infinity (e^{0.03x} -> 0) to get horizontal asymptote y = ln(1/2025) = -ln(2025)
Evaluate limit as x -> +infinity by dividing numerator & denominator by e^{0.03x} to get horizontal asymptote y = ln(5/12) = ln(5) - ln(12)
Justify why there is NO vertical asymptote because 50e^{0.03x} + 1 > 1 > 0 and 120e^{0.03x} + 2025 > 2025 > 0 for all real x
hints: Hint 1: Check **both** $x \to -\infty$ and $x \to +\infty$ separately! Exponential functions behave completely differently in the two directions (Ch. 9 & 10).
Hint 2: For $x \to +\infty$, factor out $e^{0.03x}$ inside the fraction. For vertical asymptotes, check whether the numerator or denominator inside $\ln(\cdot)$ can ever be $\le 0$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
1. **As $x \to -\infty$:** $e^{0.03x} \to 0$, so $\frac{50e^{0.03x}+1}{120e^{0.03x}+2025} \to \frac{1}{2025}$, giving:
$$\lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x) = \ln\!\left(\frac{1}{2025}\right) = -\ln(2025)$$
Thus **$y = -\ln(2025)$** is a horizontal asymptote as $x \to -\infty$.

2. **As $x \to +\infty$:** Divide numerator and denominator inside $\ln$ by $e^{0.03x}$:
$$\frac{50 + e^{-0.03x}}{120 + 2025e^{-0.03x}} \xrightarrow{x \to \infty} \frac{50}{120} = \frac{5}{12} \implies \lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = \ln(5) - \ln(12)$$
Thus **$y = \ln(5) - \ln(12)$** is a horizontal asymptote as $x \to +\infty$.

3. **Vertical asymptotes:** Since $e^{0.03x} > 0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$, both $50e^{0.03x} + 1 > 1$ and $120e^{0.03x} + 2025 > 2025$ everywhere. Neither vanishes, so $f(x)$ is defined and continuous on $\mathbb{R}$ and has **no vertical asymptote**.
questions.pitfall: Examiner report note (hardest problem on the exam, avg score 15%!): most students checked only $x \to +\infty$ and missed $x \to -\infty$, or forgot to test whether the argument of $\ln(\cdot)$ could hit $0$.

questions.title: Autumn 2024 Exam · Problem 1
questions.promptMarkdown:
We have the function $f(x) = e^{0.5x^2 - 3x}$.

**i)** Determine the derivative function $f'(x)$.

**ii)** Determine the stationary points of $f(x)$ and determine where $f(x)$ is increasing and decreasing.
rubricChecks: Apply chain rule with u(x) = 0.5x^2 - 3x to obtain f'(x) = (x - 3)e^{0.5x^2 - 3x}
Use e^{0.5x^2 - 3x} > 0 to solve f'(x) = 0 => unique stationary point x = 3
State decreasing on <-inf, 3] and increasing on [3, inf>
hints: Hint 1: Apply the chain rule with inner function $u(x) = 0.5x^2 - 3x$ and outer function $g(u) = e^u$ (Ch. 11–12).
Hint 2: Since $e^u > 0$ for all real $u$, the sign of $f'(x)$ is determined solely by $(x - 3)$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** By the chain rule with $u(x) = 0.5x^2 - 3x$ ($u'(x) = x - 3$):
$$f'(x) = (x - 3)e^{0.5x^2 - 3x}$$

**ii)** Since $e^{0.5x^2 - 3x} > 0$ for every $x \in \mathbb{R}$, $f'(x) = 0 \iff x - 3 = 0 \iff \mathbf{x = 3}$ (the unique stationary point). Moreover, $f'(x) < 0$ for $x < 3$ and $f'(x) > 0$ for $x > 3$, so $f(x)$ is **decreasing for $x \in \langle -\infty, 3]$** and **increasing for $x \in [3, \infty\rangle$**.
questions.pitfall: Setting $0.5x^2 - 3x = 0$ (trying to solve $e^u = 0$, which has no solutions) instead of setting $u'(x) = x - 3 = 0$.

questions.title: Autumn 2024 Exam · Problem 2
questions.promptMarkdown: Make a drawing of the ellipse given by the equation $x^2 + 9(y - 5)^2 = 36$.
rubricChecks: Divide both sides by 36 to write standard form x^2 / 6^2 + (y - 5)^2 / 2^2 = 1
Identify centre (0, 5), horizontal semi-axis a = 6, and vertical semi-axis b = 2
Draw ellipse accurately through (-6, 5), (6, 5), (0, 3), and (0, 7)
hints: Hint 1: Divide both sides by $36$ so the right-hand side equals $1$ (Ch. 8).
Hint 2: Read off $a^2 = 36 \implies a = 6$ and $b^2 = \frac{36}{9} = 4 \implies b = 2$ around centre $(0, 5)$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Dividing both sides by $36$ puts the equation in standard form:
$$\frac{x^2}{36} + \frac{(y - 5)^2}{4} = 1 \iff \frac{(x - 0)^2}{6^2} + \frac{(y - 5)^2}{2^2} = 1$$
The centre is $(0, 5)$ with horizontal semi-axis $a = 6$ and vertical semi-axis $b = 2$. Sketch the ellipse passing through $(-6, 5)$, $(6, 5)$, $(0, 3)$, and $(0, 7)$.

questions.title: Autumn 2024 Exam · Problem 4
questions.promptMarkdown:
**i)** Calculate the sum of the geometric series:
$$8\,000 \cdot 1.005^{143} + 8\,000 \cdot 1.005^{142} + 8\,000 \cdot 1.005^{141} + \cdots + 8\,000 \cdot 1.005^{25} + 8\,000 \cdot 1.005^{24}$$

**ii)** Describe a finance situation where this sum is relevant (the important numbers should be interpreted).
rubricChecks: Read backwards with first term a1 = 8000 * 1.005^24, ratio k = 1.005, and n = 143 - 24 + 1 = 120 terms

Interpret as future bank balance (e.g. 12 years from now at 6% nominal annual rate with monthly compounding 0.5%/month, 120 monthly deposits of 8,000 from month 1 to month 120 left for 24 more months)
hints: Hint 1: Read the sum from right to left so $a_1 = 8\,000 \cdot 1.005^{24}$ and $k = 1.005$, and count the terms from power $24$ to $143$ inclusive ($143 - 24 + 1 = 120$, Ch. 4).

Hint 2: Since powers are multiplied (not divided), this is a **future value**! Notice $0.005 = 0.5\%$ per month corresponds to $6\%$ nominal annual interest with monthly compounding ($144$ months $= 12$ years).
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** Reading from right to left: $a_1 = 8\,000 \cdot 1.005^{24}$, $k = 1.005$, and $n = 143 - 24 + 1 = 120$ terms:
$$S = 8\,000 \cdot 1.005^{24} \cdot \frac{1.005^{120} - 1}{0.005} \approx 1\,477\,745.66$$

**ii)** The sum is the **balance (future value) in a savings account $12$ years ($144$ months) from now** at **$6\%$ nominal annual interest with monthly compounding** ($0.5\%$ per month), when **$8\,000$ is deposited monthly for $10$ years** ($120$ deposits: first deposit $1$ month from now earning $143$ months of interest, last deposit $120$ months from now remaining in the account for $2$ more years / $24$ months).
questions.pitfall: Forgetting the factor $1.005^{24}$ in $a_1$ (treating the last term as $8\,000$ instead of $8\,000 \cdot 1.005^{24}$) or miscounting $143 - 24 = 119$ terms.

questions.title: Autumn 2024 Exam · Problem 5
questions.promptMarkdown: The hyperbola function $f(x)$ has graph as in Figure 2. Determine the expression of the hyperbola function.
rubricChecks: Identify asymptote intersection / symmetry centre (b, c) = (30, 50) from the graph
Read a clean lattice point on the curve such as (32, 52) or (28, 48) (or (34, 51))
hints: Hint 1: Read the vertical asymptote $x = b$ and horizontal asymptote $y = c$ from Figure 2 to write $f(x) = c + \frac{a}{x - b}$ (Ch. 9).
Hint 2: Pick an exact grid intersection point on one branch — such as $(32, 52)$, $(34, 51)$, or $(28, 48)$ — to solve for $a$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
From Figure 2, the vertical asymptote is $x = 30$ and the horizontal asymptote is $y = 50$ (symmetry centre $(30, 50)$), so:
$$f(x) = 50 + \frac{a}{x - 30}$$
The curve passes cleanly through the grid point $(32, 52)$ (and $(28, 48)$, $(34, 51)$). Substituting $f(32) = 52$:
$$50 + \frac{a}{32 - 30} = 52 \implies \frac{a}{2} = 2 \implies a = 4$$
Hence **$f(x) = 50 + \dfrac{4}{x - 30}$**.
questions.pitfall: Reading an approximate non-lattice point instead of exact grid intersections $(32, 52)$ and $(28, 48)$, or getting the sign of $a$ wrong.

questions.title: Autumn 2024 Exam · Problem 6
questions.promptMarkdown: Determine the expression of the second degree polynomial function $f(x)$ if the graph passes through the point $P = (10, 20)$ and has maximum point $Q = (12, 24)$.
rubricChecks: Use vertex form f(x) = a(x - 12)^2 + 24 from maximum point Q = (12, 24)
hints: Hint 1: A quadratic with maximum point $(s, d) = (12, 24)$ immediately has standard vertex form $f(x) = a(x - 12)^2 + 24$ with $a < 0$ (Ch. 8).
Hint 2: Plug in $f(10) = 20$ to solve for $a$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Using standard vertex form $f(x) = a(x - s)^2 + d$ with maximum point $(s, d) = (12, 24)$:
$$f(x) = a(x - 12)^2 + 24$$
Inserting $P = (10, 20)$ gives $a(10 - 12)^2 + 24 = 20 \implies 4a = -4 \implies a = -1$. Thus:
$$f(x) = -(x - 12)^2 + 24 \quad (= -x^2 + 24x - 120)$$
questions.pitfall: Examiner report note (avg score 48%): setting up three messy equations in $ax^2 + bx + c$ and making arithmetic errors instead of using vertex form $a(x - 12)^2 + 24$.

questions.title: Autumn 2024 Exam · Problem 8
questions.promptMarkdown:
Let $p$ be the price of a commodity and assume $D(p) = -\ln(p)$ with $0 < p < 1$ is the demand function. Let $\varepsilon(p)$ be the momentary price elasticity of the demand function.

**i)** Calculate $\varepsilon(p)$.

**ii)** Determine the price $p$ such that the demand is elastic.

**iii)** Determine whether the revenue is increasing or decreasing if the price increases a little from $p = 0.5$.
rubricChecks: Differentiate D'(p) = -1/p and simplify epsilon(p) = (-1/p)*p / (-ln p) = 1 / ln(p)
Solve 1 / ln(p) < -1 on 0 < p < 1 (noting ln(p) < 0 flips inequality!) to get ln(p) > -1 => p in <e^{-1}, 1>
Compare p = 0.5 > e^{-1} ≈ 0.368 so demand is elastic and revenue decreases when price rises slightly from 0.5
hints: Hint 1: Remember that for $0 < p < 1$, $\ln(p)$ is **negative**, so $D(p) = -\ln(p) > 0$ and $\varepsilon(p) = \frac{1}{\ln(p)} < 0$ (Ch. 7, 10 & 17).
Hint 2: When solving $\frac{1}{\ln(p)} < -1$, multiplying both sides by $\ln(p) < 0$ **reverses** the inequality sign (or bring $+1$ to the left as $\frac{\ln(p)+1}{\ln(p)} < 0$).
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** Since $D'(p) = -\frac{1}{p}$, we obtain:
$$\varepsilon(p) = \frac{D'(p) \cdot p}{D(p)} = \frac{(-1/p) \cdot p}{-\ln(p)} = \frac{1}{\ln(p)}$$

**ii)** Demand is elastic when $\varepsilon(p) < -1$, i.e. $\frac{1}{\ln(p)} < -1 \iff \frac{\ln(p) + 1}{\ln(p)} < 0$. Because $\ln(p) < 0$ for all $0 < p < 1$, the numerator must be positive:
$$\ln(p) + 1 > 0 \iff \ln(p) > -1 \iff p > e^{-1}$$
Combining with $0 < p < 1$ gives **$p \in \langle e^{-1}, 1\rangle$** ($e^{-1} \approx 0.3679$).

**iii)** Since $0.5 > e^{-1} \approx 0.3679$, demand is elastic at $p = 0.5$, so a small price increase from $0.5$ **decreases revenue**.
questions.pitfall: Examiner report trap (avg score 45%): multiplying $\frac{1}{\ln(p)} < -1$ by $\ln(p)$ without flipping the inequality sign (forgetting $\ln(p) < 0$ on $\langle 0, 1\rangle$).

questions.title: Autumn 2024 Exam · Problem 9
questions.promptMarkdown:
The second derivative of the function $f(x)$ is given as the following function:
$$f''(x) = (e^x - 7)\ln(x^2 + 0.5)$$
**i)** Determine the inflection points of $f(x)$.

**ii)** Determine where $f(x)$ is convex and concave.
rubricChecks: Construct a complete sign diagram for f''(x) ordering -1/sqrt(2) < 1/sqrt(2) < ln(7)
Identify all three inflection points and state exact concave and convex intervals
hints: Hint 1: $f''(x)$ is already given! Do **not** differentiate again — instead find the zeros of each factor $e^x - 7 = 0$ and $\ln(x^2 + 0.5) = 0$ (Ch. 10 & 14).

Hint 2: Remember $\ln(u) = 0 \iff u = 1$, so $x^2 + 0.5 = 1 \iff x^2 = 0.5$. Check the numerical ordering: $-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \approx -0.71$, $+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.71$, and $\ln(7) \approx 1.95$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Find the zeros of $f''(x)$ (defined for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ since $x^2 + 0.5 \ge 0.5 > 0$):
- $e^x - 7 = 0 \iff x = \ln(7) \approx 1.95$ (negative to the left, positive to the right).
- $\ln(x^2 + 0.5) = 0 \iff x^2 + 0.5 = 1 \iff x^2 = \frac{1}{2} \iff x = \pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \approx \pm 0.71$ (negative on $\langle -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\rangle$, positive outside).

Sign diagram of $f''(x) = (e^x - 7)\ln(x^2 + 0.5)$:
- $x < -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$: $(-)(+) = - < 0$ (concave)
- $-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} < x < \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$: $(-)(-) = + > 0$ (convex)
- $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} < x < \ln(7)$: $(-)(+) = - < 0$ (concave)
- $x > \ln(7)$: $(+)(+) = + > 0$ (convex)

**i)** Inflection points: **$x = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, $x = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, and $x = \ln(7)$**.

**ii)** $f(x)$ is **concave** on $\langle -\infty, -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}]$ and $[\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \ln(7)]$, and **convex** on $[-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}]$ and $[\ln(7), \infty\rangle$.
questions.pitfall: Examiner report trap (avg score 43%): differentiating the already-given $f''(x)$ (computing $f'''(x)$!), or solving $\ln(x^2+0.5)=0$ as $x^2+0.5=0$ instead of $x^2+0.5=1$.

questions.title: Autumn 2024 Exam · Problem 10
questions.promptMarkdown:
Here are some payments at different times:

| Year | $3$ | $4$ | $5$ |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Payment | $A$ | $B$ | $C$ |

Assume the nominal discount rate is $r$ with continuous compounding.

**i)** Write up an expression for the present value of the cash flow.

**ii)** Assume $A = 40$, $B = 60$, $C = 100$. Determine $r$ such that the present value of payment $C$ is greater than the present value of payment $B$.
rubricChecks: Discount each payment continuously: PV = A*e^{-3r} + B*e^{-4r} + C*e^{-5r}
Set up inequality 100*e^{-5r} > 60*e^{-4r} and multiply by e^{5r}/60 > 0
hints: Hint 1: Under continuous compounding at nominal rate $r$, a payment $K$ in $t$ years has present value $Ke^{-rt} = \frac{K}{e^{rt}}$ (Ch. 3 & 4).
Hint 2: Since $e^{5r} > 0$ for all real $r$, multiply $\frac{100}{e^{5r}} > \frac{60}{e^{4r}}$ by $\frac{e^{5r}}{60}$ to isolate $e^r$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** Discounting each payment with continuous compounding factor $e^{-rt}$:
$$\text{PV} = \frac{A}{e^{3r}} + \frac{B}{e^{4r}} + \frac{C}{e^{5r}} = Ae^{-3r} + Be^{-4r} + Ce^{-5r}$$

**ii)** We solve $\frac{100}{e^{5r}} > \frac{60}{e^{4r}}$. Multiplying both sides by $\frac{e^{5r}}{60} > 0$ gives:
$$\frac{100}{60} > e^r \iff e^r < \frac{5}{3} \iff r < \ln(5) - \ln(3) \approx 0.5108 = \mathbf{51.08\%}$$
questions.pitfall: Using discrete discounting $\frac{A}{(1+r)^3}$ when the prompt explicitly specifies **continuous compounding**.

questions.title: Autumn 2024 Exam · Problem 11
questions.promptMarkdown:
We have the function $f(x) = \dfrac{60e^{-0.01x} + 100}{e^{-0.01x} + 4}$ with domain of definition $D_f = [0, \infty\rangle$. Let $g(x)$ be the inverse function of $f(x)$.

**i)** Determine the expression of $g(x)$.

**ii)** Determine the domain of definition $D_g$ and the range $R_g$ of $g(x)$.
rubricChecks: Isolate e^{-0.01x} = (4y - 100)/(60 - y) by clearing denominator and grouping e^{-0.01x} terms
Take ln and swap x, y to obtain g(x) = -100 * ln((4x - 100)/(60 - x))
Prove f is decreasing on [0, inf> with f(0) = 32 and lim_{x->inf} f(x) = 25, giving D_g = R_f = <25, 32] and R_g = D_f = [0, inf>
hints: Hint 1: Set $y = \frac{60e^{-0.01x}+100}{e^{-0.01x}+4}$, multiply by $(e^{-0.01x}+4)$, and collect every term containing $e^{-0.01x}$ on one side (Ch. 10).

Hint 2: Do NOT read $D_g$ from the formula for $g(x)$ alone (which would give $\langle 25, 60\rangle$)! Because $D_f = [0, \infty\rangle$, compute $f(0)$ and $\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x)$ to get the actual range $D_g = R_f$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** Solve $y = \frac{60e^{-0.01x}+100}{e^{-0.01x}+4}$ for $x$:
$$y(e^{-0.01x} + 4) = 60e^{-0.01x} + 100 \implies 4y - 100 = (60 - y)e^{-0.01x} \implies e^{-0.01x} = \frac{4y - 100}{60 - y}$$
Taking natural logarithms and multiplying by $-100$ gives $x = -100\ln\!\left(\frac{4y - 100}{60 - y}\right)$. Swapping $x$ and $y$:
$$g(x) = -100\ln\!\left(\frac{4x - 100}{60 - x}\right)$$

**ii)** Rewrite $f(x) = \frac{60(e^{-0.01x}+4) - 140}{e^{-0.01x}+4} = 60 - \frac{140}{e^{-0.01x}+4}$ (or compute $f'(x) = \frac{-1.4e^{-0.01x}}{(e^{-0.01x}+4)^2} < 0$), so $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing on $D_f = [0, \infty\rangle$.
- At $x = 0$: $f(0) = \frac{60 + 100}{1 + 4} = 32$.
- As $x \to \infty$: $e^{-0.01x} \to 0^+$, so $f(x) \to \frac{100}{4} = 25^+$.

Hence **$D_g = R_f = \langle 25, 32]$** and **$R_g = D_f = [0, \infty\rangle$**.
questions.pitfall: Examiner report trap (avg score 37%): writing $D_g = \langle 25, 60\rangle$ from the log positivity condition $\frac{4x-100}{60-x} > 0$, forgetting that $x \ge 0$ caps $f(x) \le f(0) = 32$.

questions.title: Autumn 2024 Exam · Problem 12
questions.promptMarkdown: We have the function $f(x) = \dfrac{x^3 + 7x^2 - 100x - 700}{x^2 + 2x - 35}$. Determine possible maximum and minimum on the interval $\langle 5, \infty\rangle$.
rubricChecks: Simplify f(x) on x > 5 via polynomial division (or factoring numerator (x+7)(x^2-100) and denominator (x+7)(x-5)) to f(x) = x + 5 - 75/(x - 5)
Differentiate simplified form: f'(x) = 1 + 75/(x - 5)^2
Observe f'(x) > 1 > 0 for all x > 5 (strictly increasing on an open interval) and conclude f(x) has NEITHER a maximum NOR a minimum
hints: Hint 1: Do **not** jump straight into the quotient rule on a cubic over a quadratic! Perform polynomial division (or factor $x^3+7x^2-100x-700 = x^2(x+7)-100(x+7)$ and $x^2+2x-35 = (x+7)(x-5)$) first (Ch. 6, 9 & 12)!
Hint 2: After simplifying to $f(x) = x + 5 - \frac{75}{x-5}$ for $x > 5$, check the sign of $f'(x)$ and note that $\langle 5, \infty\rangle$ has no included endpoints.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Using polynomial division (or factoring $(x+7)$ out of numerator and denominator for $x > 5$, where $x + 7 \ne 0$):
$$f(x) = \frac{(x + 7)(x^2 - 100)}{(x + 7)(x - 5)} = \frac{x^2 - 100}{x - 5} = x + 5 - \frac{75}{x - 5}$$
Differentiating for $x > 5$:
$$f'(x) = 1 + \frac{75}{(x - 5)^2} > 1 > 0$$
Because $f(x)$ is strictly increasing on the open interval $\langle 5, \infty\rangle$ (with $\lim_{x \to 5^+} f(x) = -\infty$ and $\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = +\infty$), $f(x)$ has **neither a maximum nor a minimum** on $\langle 5, \infty\rangle$.
questions.pitfall: Examiner report note (lowest score on 2024H, avg 27%!): differentiating the unsimplified cubic/quadratic quotient directly produces a degree-4 numerator where $(x+7)$ hides inside a messy expression.

questions.promptMarkdown: Determine the function expression $f(x)$ for the hyperbola in Figure 2.
rubricChecks: Read asymptotes x = 20 and y = 10 to write f(x) = 10 + a/(x - 20)
Substitute lattice point (21, 5) (or (19, 15) or (25, 9)) to obtain a = -5 and f(x) = 10 - 5/(x - 20)
hints: Hint 1: Identify the vertical asymptote $x = b$ and horizontal asymptote $y = c$ in $f(x) = c + \frac{a}{x - b}$ (Ch. 9).
Hint 2: Use a crisp grid intersection on the curve such as $(21, 5)$, $(25, 9)$, or $(19, 15)$ to find $a$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
The asymptotes intersect at $(20, 10)$, giving $f(x) = 10 + \frac{a}{x - 20}$. Since $(21, 5)$ lies on the graph, $f(21) = 10 + \frac{a}{21 - 20} = 5 \implies a = -5$. Hence:
$$f(x) = 10 - \frac{5}{x - 20}$$
questions.pitfall: Missing the negative sign on $a = -5$ (note the branches lie in the top-left and bottom-right quadrants relative to $(20, 10)$).

questions.promptMarkdown: Find an expression for the second degree polynomial function $f(x)$ if the graph has top-point $P = (6, 10)$ and passes through the point $Q = (4, 8)$.

questions.solutionMarkdown:

Hence **$f(x) = -0.5(x - 6)^2 + 10$** ($= -0.5x^2 + 6x - 8$).
questions.pitfall: Writing $(x + 6)^2$ instead of $(x - 6)^2$ in vertex form.

questions.title: Spring 2024 Exam · Problem 4
questions.promptMarkdown:
The graphs of the functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are given in Figure 3.

**i)** Use the figure to solve the inequality $f(x) \le g(x)$.

**ii)** Use the figure to solve the inequality $f(x) \cdot g(x) \ge 0$.
rubricChecks: Read intervals where graph of f lies on or below g (on visible domain [1.2, 9.3]): 1.2 <= x <= 2 or 4.4 <= x <= 7.4
Identify where f(x) and g(x) share the same sign (or either equals 0)
Include shared root x = 2 as an isolated solution alongside [4, 5] and [7, 8]
hints: Hint 1: In (i), look where the red curve $f$ is at or below the green curve $g$. In (ii), $f(x) \cdot g(x) \ge 0$ holds wherever $f$ and $g$ are **both $\ge 0$** or **both $\le 0$** relative to the $x$-axis (Ch. 7).
Hint 2: Unlike $\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} \le 0$, here we have a **product** $f(x) \cdot g(x) \ge 0$, so check $x = 2$ where $f(2) = g(2) = 0$!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** $f(x) \le g(x)$ where the graph of $f$ is on or below $g$: **$x \le 2$** (or $1.2 \le x \le 2$ on the plotted interval) **or $4.4 \le x \le 7.4$**.

**ii)** $f(x) \cdot g(x) \ge 0$ holds when both functions have the same sign or at least one is zero:
- At $x = 2$: $f(2) \cdot g(2) = 0 \cdot 0 = 0 \ge 0$ (**$x = 2$ is also a solution**, noted alongside the interval check!).
- On $[4, 5]$: $f(x) \le 0$ and $g(x) \le 0 \implies f(x)g(x) \ge 0$.
- On $[7, 8]$: $f(x) \ge 0$ and $g(x) \ge 0 \implies f(x)g(x) \ge 0$.

Thus $x \in [4, 5]$, $x \in [7, 8]$ (and the isolated root $x = 2$).
questions.pitfall: Confusing where $f$ and $g$ intersect each other (part i) with where they cross the $x$-axis $y = 0$ (part ii).

questions.title: Spring 2024 Exam · Problem 5
questions.promptMarkdown:
The graph of the function $f(x)$ is given in Figure 3 (shared with Problem 4).

**i)** Use the figure to find an approximation to $f'(4)$.

**ii)** Use the figure to make the sign-line for $f''(x)$.
questions.contextMarkdown: Shared Figure 3 from Spring 2024 Exam p. 2 (red curve is $f(x)$):
rubricChecks: Draw/follow tangent to red curve f(x) at (4, 0) and compute slope Δy/Δx ≈ -0.7
Identify inflection points of f(x) at x ≈ 4 and x ≈ 7.5
State f''(x) <= 0 for x <= 4, f''(x) >= 0 for 4 <= x <= 7.5, and f''(x) <= 0 for x >= 7.5
hints: Hint 1: For (i), trace the tangent line to the red curve $f(x)$ at $(4, 0)$ across $1$ unit in $x$ (e.g. back to $x = 3$) to estimate rise over run (Ch. 11).
Hint 2: For (ii), $f''(x) < 0$ where $f$ bends downwards (concave) and $f''(x) > 0$ where $f$ bends upwards (convex, Ch. 14).
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** Following the tangent to $f(x)$ at $(4, 0)$ backwards to $x = 3$, the tangent passes near $(3, 0.7)$, giving slope:
$$f'(4) \approx \frac{0 - 0.7}{4 - 3} = -0.7$$

**ii)** $f(x)$ bends downwards (concave) for $x < 4$, bends upwards (convex) for $4 < x < 7.5$, and bends downwards again for $x > 7.5$, with inflection points at $x \approx 4$ and $x \approx 7.5$. Thus:
- $f''(x) \le 0$ for $x \le 4$
- $f''(x) \ge 0$ for $4 \le x \le 7.5$
- $f''(x) \le 0$ for $x \ge 7.5$
questions.pitfall: Using the zeros of $f'(x)$ (peaks/troughs near $x=2.8, 5.6, 8.8$) instead of the inflection points ($x \approx 4, 7.5$) for the sign-line of $f''(x)$.

questions.title: Spring 2024 Exam · Problem 6
questions.promptMarkdown:
We have the function $f(x) = 30e^{x(10 - x)}$.

**i)** Calculate the expression for the derivative function $f'(x)$ and determine the stationary points for $f(x)$.

**ii)** Determine the maximal value and minimal value for $f(x)$ when the domain of definition for $f(x)$ is $D_f = [3, 8]$.
rubricChecks: Expand u(x) = 10x - x^2 and apply chain rule to obtain f'(x) = 60(5 - x)e^{x(10 - x)}
Find unique stationary point x = 5
Evaluate stationary point and both closed-interval endpoints: f(3) = 30e^21, f(5) = 30e^25 (max), and f(8) = 30e^16 (min)
hints: Hint 1: Expand the exponent $u(x) = x(10 - x) = 10x - x^2$ before applying the chain rule so you don't need a product rule inside the exponent (Ch. 11–12).
Hint 2: By the Extreme Value Theorem on $[3, 8]$, global extrema occur either at stationary points inside $\langle 3, 8\rangle$ or at the endpoints $x = 3$ and $x = 8$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** With inner function $u(x) = 10x - x^2$ ($u'(x) = 10 - 2x = 2(5 - x)$), the chain rule gives:
$$f'(x) = 30(10 - 2x)e^{x(10 - x)} = 60(5 - x)e^{x(10 - x)}$$
Since $e^{x(10-x)} > 0$, $f'(x) = 0 \iff x = 5$ (unique stationary point).

**ii)** On the closed bounded interval $[3, 8]$, compare $f(5)$ against the endpoint values $f(3)$ and $f(8)$:
- $f(3) = 30e^{3 \cdot 7} = 30e^{21}$
- $f(5) = 30e^{5 \cdot 5} = 30e^{25}$
- $f(8) = 30e^{8 \cdot 2} = 30e^{16}$

Since $30e^{16} < 30e^{21} < 30e^{25}$, the **maximal value is $f(5) = 30e^{25}$** and the **minimal value is $f(8) = 30e^{16}$**.
questions.pitfall: Reporting the $x$-coordinates ($5$ and $8$) when the prompt asks for the **maximal value and minimal value** ($30e^{25}$ and $30e^{16}$), or forgetting to test both endpoints.

questions.title: Spring 2024 Exam · Problem 7
questions.promptMarkdown:
Kåre is thinking about saving money, with $15\,000$ each month, with the first deposit $4$ years from now. Assume nominal interest is $6\%$ with monthly compounding. Assume last deposit is $12$ years from now.

**i)** Write up a geometric series for how much Kåre has in his account $12$ years from now.

**ii)** Calculate how much Kåre has in his account $12$ years from now.
rubricChecks: Find monthly rate 6% / 12 = 0.5% (factor 1.005) and 12 * (12 - 4) = 96 interest periods for the first deposit
Include the final deposit at t = 12 years (0 months of interest) so there are 96 + 1 = 97 deposits
hints: Hint 1: Monthly interest is $r_m = \frac{6\%}{12} = 0.5\% = 0.005$. How many months does the first deposit (at month $48$) earn interest until month $144$ ($144 - 48 = 96$, Ch. 4)?
Hint 2: Watch the fencepost count! Powers run from $1.005^{96}$ down to $1.005^0 = 1$ (the deposit made right at year $12$), which is **$97$ payments**, not $96$!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** Monthly interest rate is $6\% / 12 = 0.5\%$ ($k = 1.005$). The first deposit ($4$ years $= 48$ months from now) earns interest for $12 \cdot (12 - 4) = 96$ months, while the last deposit ($12$ years from now) earns $0$ months of interest ($97$ deposits in total):
$$15\,000 \cdot 1.005^{96} + 15\,000 \cdot 1.005^{95} + \cdots + 15\,000 \cdot 1.005 + 15\,000$$

**ii)** Reading backwards with $a_1 = 15\,000$, $k = 1.005$, and $n = 97$ terms:
$$S = 15\,000 \cdot \frac{1.005^{97} - 1}{0.005} \approx 1\,866\,640.27$$
questions.pitfall: Using $n = 12 \cdot (12 - 4) = 96$ deposits instead of $97$ (forgetting that deposits at both month $48$ and month $144$ are included).
