questions.title: Spring 2024 Exam · Problem 8
questions.promptMarkdown:
Here is a cash flow:

| Year | $0$ | $1$ | $3$ | $5$ |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Payment | $-20$ | $-20$ | $25$ | $40$ |

**i)** Write up the equation for the internal rate of return (IRR). *(Note: you are not supposed to solve the equation!)*

**ii)** Determine whether the internal rate of return is larger or smaller than $14\%$ *(Note: calculation by the finance buttons on the calculator is not a valid argument!)*.
rubricChecks: Write exact IRR equation NPV(r) = -20 - 20/(1+r) + 25/(1+r)^3 + 40/(1+r)^5 = 0
Evaluate NPV(0.14) ≈ +0.1052 > 0
Justify why NPV(r) decreases around r = 0.14 (e.g. test r = 0.1405 giving NPV ≈ +0.0452 or derivative/dominance of later positive terms) to conclude IRR > 14%
hints: Hint 1: Set $\text{NPV}(r) = 0$ keeping the exact years $0, 1, 3, 5$ in the exponents (note years $2$ and $4$ have zero payment, Ch. 3)!

Hint 2: Evaluate $\text{NPV}(0.14)$. Because the year-$1$ term $-\frac{20}{1+r}$ is negative, briefly verify (e.g. by also evaluating $\text{NPV}(0.141)$ or $\text{NPV}(0.15)$) that $\text{NPV}(r)$ decreases past $0$ for $r > 14\%$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** Setting net present value equal to zero gives the IRR equation:
$$-20 - \frac{20}{1 + r} + \frac{25}{(1 + r)^3} + \frac{40}{(1 + r)^5} = 0$$

**ii)** At $r = 0.14$:
$$\text{NPV}(0.14) = -20 - \frac{20}{1.14} + \frac{25}{1.14^3} + \frac{40}{1.14^5} \approx 0.1052 > 0$$
As $r$ increases above $14\%$, the high-power positive inflows shrink faster than $-\frac{20}{1+r}$ becomes less negative (indeed $\text{NPV}(0.1405) \approx 0.0452 > 0$ and $\text{NPV}(0.142) \approx -0.134 < 0$). By the Intermediate Value Theorem, the **IRR is larger than $14\%$** (specifically $\approx 14.09\%$).
questions.pitfall: Using exponents $1, 2, 3$ instead of $1, 3, 5$, or claiming $\text{NPV}(r)$ is automatically decreasing without addressing the negative $-20/(1+r)$ term (evaluating a second test point like $r=14.2\%$ makes the IVT proof airtight!).

questions.title: Spring 2024 Exam · Problem 9
questions.promptMarkdown:
We have the function $f(x) = 4 + 5e^{-0.1x}$ with domain of definition $D_f = [0, \infty\rangle$.

**i)** Determine the asymptotes of $f(x)$.

**ii)** Determine the inverse function $g(x)$, determine the domain of definition $D_g$, and determine the range $R_g$.
rubricChecks: State no vertical asymptote and horizontal asymptote y = 4 as x -> infinity
Use f(0) = 9 and lim_{x->inf} f(x) = 4+ on decreasing f to state D_g = <4, 9] and R_g = [0, inf>
hints: Hint 1: On $D_f = [0, \infty\rangle$, check if $f(x)$ has any vertical asymptotes and evaluate $\lim_{x \to \infty} (4 + 5e^{-0.1x})$ (Ch. 9 & 10).
Hint 2: Isolate $e^{-0.1x} = \frac{y - 4}{5}$, apply $\ln$, and find $D_g = R_f$ using $f(0) = 9$ and the horizontal asymptote $y = 4$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** $f(x)$ is continuous on $[0, \infty\rangle$, so it has **no vertical asymptotes**. Since $\lim_{x \to \infty} (4 + 5e^{-0.1x}) = 4^+$, **$y = 4$ is a horizontal asymptote**.

**ii)** Solving $y = 4 + 5e^{-0.1x}$ for $x$: $e^{-0.1x} = \frac{y - 4}{5} \implies -0.1x = \ln\!\left(\frac{y - 4}{5}\right) \implies x = -10\ln\!\left(\frac{y - 4}{5}\right) = 10\ln\!\left(\frac{5}{y - 4}\right)$. Swapping variables:
$$g(x) = 10\ln\!\left(\frac{5}{x - 4}\right) \quad \left(= -10\ln\frac{x - 4}{5}\right)$$
Since $f$ is strictly decreasing on $[0, \infty\rangle$ with $f(0) = 9$ and $\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = 4^+$, **$D_g = R_f = \langle 4, 9]$** and **$R_g = D_f = [0, \infty\rangle$**.
questions.pitfall: Writing $D_g = \langle 4, \infty\rangle$ from $x - 4 > 0$ instead of capping at $f(0) = 9$ due to $D_f = [0, \infty\rangle$.

questions.title: Spring 2024 Exam · Problem 10
questions.promptMarkdown:
**i)** Solve the equation $\ln(x^4 - x^2 - 5) = 0$.

**ii)** Use one parameter to write an expression for all polynomials on the form $x^2 + bx + c$ which have two zeros of distance $6$ from each other.
rubricChecks: Exponentiate ln(x^4 - x^2 - 5) = 0 to x^4 - x^2 - 5 = 1 => x^4 - x^2 - 6 = 0
Substitute u = x^2 >= 0: (u - 3)(u + 2) = 0 => x^2 = 3 => x = ±sqrt(3)
Parameterise roots (e.g. s - 3 and s + 3, or r and r + 6) and expand to x^2 - 2sx + (s^2 - 9)
hints: Hint 1: In (i), apply $e^{(\cdot)}$ to both sides: $\ln(A) = 0 \iff A = e^0 = 1$, then substitute $u = x^2$ (Ch. 5 & 10).
Hint 2: In (ii), let the midpoint (symmetry axis) be $s$ so the two roots are $s - 3$ and $s + 3$, then expand $(x - (s-3))(x - (s+3))$!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** Exponentiating both sides gives $x^4 - x^2 - 5 = e^0 = 1 \implies x^4 - x^2 - 6 = 0$. Let $u = x^2$:
$$u^2 - u - 6 = 0 \implies (u - 3)(u + 2) = 0$$
Since $x^2 = -2$ has no real solutions, $x^2 = 3 \implies \mathbf{x = \pm\sqrt{3}}$.

**ii)** Let $s \in \mathbb{R}$ be the midpoint between the two zeros, so the zeros are $s - 3$ and $s + 3$ (distance $(s+3) - (s-3) = 6$). Factorised and expanded:
$$(x - (s - 3))(x - (s + 3)) = ((x - s) + 3)((x - s) - 3) = (x - s)^2 - 9 = x^2 - 2sx + s^2 - 9$$
(Equivalently, choosing parameter $r$ as the smaller root gives $(x - r)(x - r - 6) = x^2 - (2r + 6)x + r(r + 6)$.)
questions.pitfall: Solving $\ln(x^4 - x^2 - 5) = 0$ by setting $x^4 - x^2 - 5 = 0$ instead of $e^0 = 1$.

questions.title: Spring 2024 Exam · Problem 12
questions.promptMarkdown:
An amount $K_0$ is deposited in an account today and increases to $K_{10}$ in $10$ years.

**i)** Find an expression for the effective annual interest $r_{\text{eff}}$.

**ii)** Assume there is continuous compounding. Find an expression for the nominal annual interest $r$.
rubricChecks: Set up K_10 = K_0 * (1 + r_eff)^10 and solve r_eff = (K_10 / K_0)^(1/10) - 1
Set up e^{10r} = K_10 / K_0 (or e^r = 1 + r_eff) for continuous compounding
hints: Hint 1: By definition of effective annual interest, $K_{10} = K_0(1 + r_{\text{eff}})^{10}$; solve symbolically for $r_{\text{eff}}$ using the $\frac{1}{10}$ power (Ch. 2 & 4).
Hint 2: Under continuous compounding, $K_{10} = K_0 e^{10r}$ (equivalently $e^r = 1 + r_{\text{eff}}$); solve for $r$ using $\ln$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** From $K_{10} = K_0 (1 + r_{\text{eff}})^{10}$, divide by $K_0$ and raise both sides to the power $\frac{1}{10}$:
$$(1 + r_{\text{eff}})^{10} = \frac{K_{10}}{K_0} \implies r_{\text{eff}} = \left(\frac{K_{10}}{K_0}\right)^{\frac{1}{10}} - 1$$

**ii)** With continuous compounding, the annual growth factor is $e^r = 1 + r_{\text{eff}} = \left(\frac{K_{10}}{K_0}\right)^{1/10}$. Taking natural logarithms:
$$r = \ln(1 + r_{\text{eff}}) = \frac{1}{10}\ln\!\left(\frac{K_{10}}{K_0}\right) = \frac{1}{10}(\ln K_{10} - \ln K_0)$$
questions.pitfall: Leaving $1 + r_{\text{eff}}$ without subtracting $1$, or dividing $\frac{K_{10}}{K_0}$ by $10$ instead of taking the $10$-th root.

questions.title: Autumn 2023 Exam · Problem 2
questions.promptMarkdown:
Calculate the expression for the derivative function $f'(x)$ if:

**i)** $f(x) = 12xe^x$  
**ii)** $f(x) = \dfrac{36 - 4x}{x - 7}$  
**iii)** $f(x) = \ln(x^{50})$
rubricChecks: Apply product rule on (i): f'(x) = 12e^x + 12xe^x = 12(1 + x)e^x
Apply quotient rule on (ii): f'(x) = (-4(x - 7) - (36 - 4x)) / (x - 7)^2 = -8 / (x - 7)^2
Differentiate (iii) via chain rule 50x^49 / x^50 = 50/x (or log rule ln(x^50) = 50 ln|x| for x ≠ 0 => f'(x) = 50/x)
hints: Hint 1: Use the product rule on (i), the quotient rule on (ii), and either a log power rule or the chain rule on (iii) (Ch. 10 & 11).
Hint 2: In (ii), watch the signs in $-4(x-7) - (36-4x) = -4x + 28 - 36 + 4x = -8$. In (iii), note $x^{50} > 0$ for all $x \ne 0$, so $\ln(x^{50}) = 50\ln|x|$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** Product rule: $f'(x) = (12x)'e^x + 12x(e^x)' = 12e^x + 12xe^x = \mathbf{12(1 + x)e^x}$.

**ii)** Quotient rule: $f'(x) = \frac{-4(x - 7) - (36 - 4x)\cdot 1}{(x - 7)^2} = \frac{-4x + 28 - 36 + 4x}{(x - 7)^2} = \mathbf{\frac{-8}{(x - 7)^2}}$.

**iii)** For all $x \ne 0$, $\ln(x^{50}) = 50\ln|x|$ (or directly by the chain rule $\frac{50x^{49}}{x^{50}}$), giving **$f'(x) = \dfrac{50}{x}$**.
questions.pitfall: Writing $\ln(x^{50}) = 50\ln(x)$ without absolute values restricts the domain to $x > 0$ when $x^{50} > 0$ is actually defined for all $x \ne 0$ (though both give $f'(x) = 50/x$).

questions.title: Autumn 2023 Exam · Problem 3
questions.promptMarkdown:
We have the function $f(x) = \dfrac{36 - 4x}{x - 7}$.

**i)** Determine the asymptotes for $f(x)$.

**ii)** Draw a sketch of the graph of $f(x)$ with asymptotes.
rubricChecks: Rewrite f(x) = -4 + 8/(x - 7) (or evaluate limits) to find vertical asymptote x = 7 and horizontal asymptote y = -4
Compute a small table of values on both sides of x = 7 (e.g. x = -1, 3, 5, 9, 11, 15)
Sketch both hyperbola branches in the correct quadrants together with dashed lines x = 7 and y = -4
hints: Hint 1: Divide $(36 - 4x)$ by $(x - 7)$ (note $-4x + 36 = -4(x - 7) + 8$) to put the hyperbola into standard form $c + \frac{a}{x - b}$ (Ch. 9).
Hint 2: Always compute $2$–$3$ clean test points on each side of $x = 7$ (such as $x = 5, 6, 8, 9$) so your branches sit in the right quadrants!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** By polynomial division, $f(x) = \frac{-4(x - 7) + 8}{x - 7} = -4 + \frac{8}{x - 7}$. Thus the **vertical asymptote is $x = 7$** and the **horizontal asymptote is $y = -4$**.

**ii)** Symmetry centre is $(7, -4)$. Sample points: $(-1, -5)$, $(3, -6)$, $(5, -8)$ on the left branch; $(9, 0)$, $(11, -2)$, $(15, -3)$ on the right branch. Draw dashed lines $x = 7$ and $y = -4$ and plot both smooth decreasing branches (lower-left and upper-right relative to $(7, -4)$).
questions.pitfall: Misreading $\frac{36 - 4x}{x - 7}$ as having horizontal asymptote $y = 36$ because $36$ is written before $-4x$ in the numerator!

questions.title: Autumn 2023 Exam · Problem 4
questions.promptMarkdown:
**i)** Solve the inequality $\ln(x + 5) \ge 3$.

**ii)** Determine which of the numbers $1.24^{100\,000}$ and $1.02^{1\,200\,000}$ is the larger.
rubricChecks: Apply strictly increasing e^u to ln(x + 5) >= 3 to get x + 5 >= e^3 => x >= e^3 - 5
Compare 1.24^100000 vs (1.02^12)^100000 (or monthly vs annual compounding at 24% nominal over 100,000 years)
Conclude 1.02^1200000 is larger because 1.02^12 ≈ 1.2682 > 1.24
hints: Hint 1: In (i), insert both sides into $e^{(\cdot)}$ and state why the inequality sign stays $\ge$ ($e^x$ is strictly increasing, Ch. 7 & 10).
Hint 2: In (ii), rewrite $1.02^{1\,200\,000} = (1.02^{12})^{100\,000}$ (or interpret both as $24\%$ nominal interest over $100\,000$ years: annual vs monthly compounding, Ch. 2).
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** Because $e^x$ is strictly increasing, $\ln(x + 5) \ge 3 \iff e^{\ln(x+5)} \ge e^3 \iff x + 5 \ge e^3$ (which automatically satisfies $x + 5 > 0$). Hence **$x \ge e^3 - 5$** ($\approx 15.09$).

**ii)** Rewrite $1.02^{1\,200\,000} = (1.02^{12})^{100\,000} \approx 1.2682^{100\,000} > 1.24^{100\,000}$ (equivalently, $24\%$ nominal interest over $100\,000$ years yields more under monthly compounding than annual compounding). Thus **$1.02^{1\,200\,000}$ is larger**.
questions.pitfall: Trying to type $1.24^{100\,000}$ directly into a calculator (overflow error) instead of factoring out the exponent $100\,000$.

questions.title: Autumn 2023 Exam · Problem 5
questions.promptMarkdown:
Here is a cash flow:

| Year | $0$ | $5$ | $6$ |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Payment | $-20$ | $10$ | $25$ |

**i)** Write up the equation for the internal rate of return. *(Note: you are not supposed to solve the equation!)*

**ii)** Determine whether the internal rate of return is larger or smaller than $10\%$ *(Note: calculation by the finance buttons on the calculator is not a valid argument!)*.
rubricChecks: Write exact IRR equation -20 + 10/(1 + r)^5 + 25/(1 + r)^6 = 0
Explain that future positive inflows decrease strictly as r increases for r > -1, so IRR > 10%
hints: Hint 1: Set $\text{NPV}(r) = 0$ using exponents $5$ and $6$ matching the table years (Ch. 3).
Hint 2: Compute $\text{NPV}(0.10)$ and explain how $\text{NPV}(r)$ changes when $r$ increases (since all future cash flows are positive, higher $r$ strictly reduces $\text{NPV}(r)$).
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** Setting net present value to zero gives:
$$-20 + \frac{10}{(1 + r)^5} + \frac{25}{(1 + r)^6} = 0$$

**ii)** Inserting $r = 0.10$ into the left-hand side gives:
$$\text{NPV}(0.10) = -20 + \frac{10}{1.10^5} + \frac{25}{1.10^6} \approx -20 + 6.209 + 14.112 = 0.321 > 0$$
Since both future payments ($10$ and $25$) are positive, $\text{NPV}(r)$ is strictly decreasing for $r > -1$. To bring $\text{NPV}(r)$ down from $+0.321$ to $0$, $r$ must increase, so the **IRR is larger than $10\%$**.
questions.pitfall: Examiner report note (avg score 53%): computing $\text{NPV}(0.10) = 0.321 > 0$ and concluding IRR $< 10\%$ (backwards!) or omitting the monotonicity argument.

questions.title: Autumn 2023 Exam · Problem 6
questions.promptMarkdown:
Draw a sketch of the graphs of the functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ with the given data. *(Note: you are not supposed to find any function expressions!)*

**i)** $f(3) = 10$, $f(9) = 15$, $f(15) = 20$, $f'(6) = -1$, $f'(12) = 1$.

**ii)** $g'(x) < 0$ for all $x$ between $20$ and $100$, $g''(x) > 0$ for all $x$ between $20$ and $60$, $g''(x) < 0$ for all $x$ between $60$ and $100$.
rubricChecks: Sketch f(x) passing through (3, 10), (9, 15), (15, 20) while bending up above 15 before x = 6 (so f'(6) = -1 < 0) and dipping below 15 before x = 12 (so f'(12) = 1 > 0)
Sketch g(x) on [20, 100] strictly decreasing everywhere with convex curvature on (20, 60), inflection at x = 60, and concave curvature on (60, 100)
hints: Hint 1: In (i), $(3,10), (9,15), (15,20)$ lie on an upward line, YET $f'(6) = -1$! How can a smooth curve climb from $10$ at $x=3$ to $15$ at $x=9$ while falling at $x=6$? Overshoot above $15$ (e.g. peak near $x=5$) before descending through $x=6$ (Ch. 11 & 14)!
Hint 2: In (ii), draw a curve on $[20, 100]$ that falls everywhere, cupping upwards on $\langle 20, 60\rangle$ and arching downwards on $\langle 60, 100\rangle$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** Plot $(3, 10)$, $(9, 15)$, and $(15, 20)$. Because $f'(6) = -1 < 0$, let $f(x)$ rise steeply from $(3,10)$ to a local peak above $20$ around $x \approx 5$, descend with slope $-1$ at $x = 6$ through $(9, 15)$ to a local trough around $x \approx 11$, and then rise with slope $+1$ at $x = 12$ up to $(15, 20)$.

**ii)** On $[20, 100]$, draw $g(x)$ strictly decreasing ($g'(x) < 0$), convex (flattening descent) on $\langle 20, 60\rangle$, passing smoothly through an inflection point at $x = 60$, and concave (steepening descent) on $\langle 60, 100\rangle$.
questions.pitfall: Drawing straight line segments through $(3, 10), (9, 15), (15, 20)$ in (i), which forces positive slope everywhere and contradicts $f'(6) = -1$.

questions.title: Autumn 2023 Exam · Problem 7
questions.promptMarkdown:
In Figure 1 you see the graph of the **derivative function** $f'(x)$. Determine whether each statement is **true** or **false**. Give a short explanation.

**i)** $f(9) > f(11)$.

**ii)** $f(x)$ has three stationary points in the interval $[2, 8]$.

**iii)** $f(x)$ has three inflection points in the interval $[2, 11]$.
rubricChecks: Conclude (i) FALSE because f'(x) > 0 (at least ~0.6) throughout [9, 11], so f is strictly increasing and f(9) < f(11)
Conclude (ii) TRUE because f'(x) = 0 (x-intercepts of the plotted curve!) occurs three times in [2, 8]: x ≈ 2.4, 4.2, and 7
Conclude (iii) TRUE because inflection points of f occur at local extrema of f'(x), which happen three times in [2, 11]: x ≈ 3, 5.3, and 9.4
hints: Hint 1: Read the caption twice! Figure 1 shows **$f'(x)$**, NOT $f(x)$ (compare with Autumn 2025 Problem 3 which used the same curve for $f(x)$!).

Hint 2: On a graph of $f'(x)$: $f$ increases where $f' > 0$ (above the $x$-axis), stationary points of $f$ are **$x$-intercepts** of $f'$, and inflection points of $f$ are **peaks/troughs** of $f'$ (Ch. 12 & 14).
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i) FALSE.** On $[9, 11]$, the plotted curve $f'(x)$ is strictly positive ($f'(x) \ge 0.6 > 0$), so $f(x)$ is strictly increasing on $[9, 11]$ and $f(9) < f(11)$.

**ii) TRUE.** Stationary points of $f(x)$ satisfy $f'(x) = 0$, which are the $x$-intercepts of the plotted $f'(x)$ curve. In $[2, 8]$ there are three: $x \approx 2.4$, $x \approx 4.2$, and $x \approx 7$.

**iii) TRUE.** Inflection points of $f(x)$ occur where $f''(x) = (f'(x))'$ changes sign, i.e. at local maxima and minima of $f'(x)$. In $[2, 11]$ there are three: $x \approx 3$ (max), $x \approx 5.3$ (min), and $x \approx 9.4$ (max).
questions.pitfall: Reading the graph as $f(x)$ instead of $f'(x)$ reverses every single answer!

questions.title: Autumn 2023 Exam · Problem 8
questions.promptMarkdown:
We have the cost function $C(x) = 3x + 100e^{rx}$ with $x \ge 0$ where $r$ is an undetermined positive number (a parameter).

**i)** Determine the marginal cost function.

**ii)** Determine the cost optimum and the minimal average unit cost.
rubricChecks: Differentiate w.r.t. x (treating r as constant parameter) to get C'(x) = 3 + 100r*e^{rx}
Set C'(x) = A(x) = (3x + 100e^{rx})/x (justified by C''(x) = 100r^2*e^{rx} > 0) and solve 100r*x*e^{rx} = 100e^{rx} => x = 1/r
Evaluate minimal average unit cost A(1/r) = C'(1/r) = 3 + 100r*e
hints: Hint 1: Treat $r > 0$ as a constant parameter when differentiating with respect to $x$: $(100e^{rx})' = 100re^{rx}$ (Ch. 11 & 16).
Hint 2: Since $C''(x) = 100r^2 e^{rx} > 0$, solve $C'(x) = \frac{C(x)}{x}$: notice $3$ cancels on both sides and $100e^{rx} > 0$ cancels cleanly!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** Differentiating with respect to $x$ (chain rule on $e^{rx}$):
$$C'(x) = 3 + 100re^{rx}$$

**ii)** Since $C''(x) = 100r^2e^{rx} > 0$ ($C$ is strictly convex), cost optimum solves $C'(x) = A(x) = \frac{3x + 100e^{rx}}{x} = 3 + \frac{100e^{rx}}{x}$:
$$3 + 100re^{rx} = 3 + \frac{100e^{rx}}{x} \implies 100rx e^{rx} = 100e^{rx} \implies rx = 1 \implies \mathbf{x = r^{-1} = \frac{1}{r}}$$
Minimal average unit cost is:
$$A(r^{-1}) = C'(r^{-1}) = 3 + 100r e^{r \cdot r^{-1}} = \mathbf{3 + 100er}$$
questions.pitfall: Examiner report note (avg score 51%): getting intimidated by parameter $r$ or forgetting to substitute $x = 1/r$ back into $A(x)$ to find minimal average unit cost $3 + 100er$.

questions.title: Autumn 2023 Exam · Problem 9
questions.promptMarkdown:
Let $p$ be the price of a commodity and suppose $D(p) = 7(p - 60)^2$ with $0 < p < 60$ is the demand function. Suppose $\varepsilon(p)$ is the momentary price elasticity of the demand function.

**i)** Calculate $\varepsilon(p)$.

**ii)** Determine whether the revenue is increasing or decreasing if the price increases a little from $p = 24$.
rubricChecks: Compute D'(p) = 14(p - 60) and simplify epsilon(p) = 14(p - 60)p / (7(p - 60)^2) = 2p / (p - 60)
Conclude demand is elastic at p = 24 so revenue decreases when price increases slightly
hints: Hint 1: Differentiate $D(p) = 7(p - 60)^2$ using the chain rule (no need to expand the square!) so $(p - 60)$ cancels cleanly in $\varepsilon(p) = \frac{D'(p)p}{D(p)}$ (Ch. 17).
Hint 2: Evaluate $\varepsilon(24)$ and compare with $-1$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** Since $D'(p) = 14(p - 60)$, we get:
$$\varepsilon(p) = \frac{D'(p) \cdot p}{D(p)} = \frac{14(p - 60)p}{7(p - 60)^2} = \frac{2p}{p - 60}$$

**ii)** At $p = 24$, $\varepsilon(24) = \frac{48}{24 - 60} = \frac{48}{-36} = -\frac{4}{3} \approx -1.33 < -1$. Demand is price elastic at $p = 24$, so **revenue decreases** if the price increases slightly from $24$.
questions.pitfall: Expanding $7(p-60)^2$ and leaving $\varepsilon(p)$ unfactored makes arithmetic slips at $p = 24$ much more likely.

questions.title: Autumn 2023 Exam · Problem 11
questions.promptMarkdown:
We have a curve $C$ given by the equation
$$x^3 - 4xy + y^2 = 0$$
**i)** Use implicit differentiation to express $y'$ in terms of $y$ and $x$.

**ii)** Determine all solutions for $y$ given that $x = 3$ and determine the slopes of the tangents to $C$ in those points.
rubricChecks: Differentiate implicitly: 3x^2 - 4y - 4xy' + 2yy' = 0 => y' = (3x^2 - 4y) / (4x - 2y)
Substitute x = 3 into 27 - 12y + y^2 = 0 to find both solutions y = 3 and y = 9
Compute tangent slopes y'(3, 9) = -9 / -6 = 1.5 and y'(3, 3) = 15 / 6 = 2.5
hints: Hint 1: Apply the product rule to $-4xy$ ($-4y - 4xy'$) and the chain rule to $y^2$ ($2yy'$), then solve for $y'$ (Ch. 13).
Hint 2: Substitute $x = 3$ into $x^3 - 4xy + y^2 = 0$ to solve the quadratic $y^2 - 12y + 27 = 0$, then evaluate $y'$ at each $(3, y)$ pair.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** Differentiating $x^3 - 4xy + y^2 = 0$ implicitly with respect to $x$:
$$3x^2 - 4y - 4xy' + 2yy' = 0 \implies (4x - 2y)y' = 3x^2 - 4y \implies y' = \frac{3x^2 - 4y}{4x - 2y}$$

**ii)** Setting $x = 3$ in the curve equation gives $27 - 12y + y^2 = 0 \iff (y - 3)(y - 9) = 0$, so **$y = 3$ or $y = 9$**.
- At $(3, 9)$: $y' = \frac{27 - 36}{12 - 18} = \frac{-9}{-6} = \mathbf{1.5}$.
- At $(3, 3)$: $y' = \frac{27 - 12}{12 - 6} = \frac{15}{6} = \mathbf{2.5}$.
questions.pitfall: Missing $-4y$ when differentiating $-4xy$, or finding only one of the two $y$-coordinates at $x = 3$.

questions.title: Autumn 2023 Exam · Problem 12
questions.promptMarkdown:
We have the function $f(x) = \dfrac{100\ln(x)}{5\ln(x) + 10}$ with domain of definition $D_f = \langle e^{-2}, \infty\rangle$.

**i)** Determine the asymptotes of $f(x)$.

**ii)** Determine the inverse function $g(x)$ with domain of definition $D_g$ and range $R_g$.
rubricChecks: Check x -> (e^{-2})+ (denominator -> 0+, numerator -> -200 => f(x) -> -inf) to get vertical asymptote x = e^{-2}
Evaluate lim_{x->inf} f(x) = 100/5 = 20 (via L'Hôpital or dividing by ln x) to get horizontal asymptote y = 20
Solve y = 100 ln(x) / (5 ln(x) + 10) for x to get g(x) = e^{2x / (20 - x)} with D_g = <-inf, 20> and R_g = <e^{-2}, inf>
hints: Hint 1: Check the left domain boundary $x \to (e^{-2})^+$ (note $5\ln(e^{-2}) + 10 = 0$) and $x \to \infty$ (either divide top & bottom by $\ln(x)$ or apply L'Hôpital's rule, Ch. 9, 10 & 15).
Hint 2: In (ii), first solve for $u = \ln(x)$ from $y = \frac{100u}{5u + 10}$ just like a rational hyperbola, then exponentiate $x = e^u$!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** As $x \to (e^{-2})^+$, $5\ln(x) + 10 \to 0^+$ while $100\ln(x) \to -200$, so $f(x) \to -\infty$ and **$x = e^{-2}$ is a vertical asymptote**. As $x \to \infty$, $\ln(x) \to \infty$, so by L'Hôpital's rule (or dividing by $\ln x$):
$$\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{100\ln(x)}{5\ln(x) + 10} = \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{100/x}{5/x} = 20$$
Hence **$y = 20$ is a horizontal asymptote**.

**ii)** Solving $y = \frac{100\ln(x)}{5\ln(x)+10}$ for $\ln(x)$:
$$5y\ln(x) + 10y = 100\ln(x) \implies (100 - 5y)\ln(x) = 10y \implies \ln(x) = \frac{10y}{100 - 5y} = \frac{2y}{20 - y}$$
Exponentiating and swapping variables gives **$g(x) = e^{\frac{2x}{20 - x}}$**. Since $f(x) = 20 - \frac{40}{\ln(x) + 2}$ is strictly increasing from $-\infty$ to $20$ on $\langle e^{-2}, \infty\rangle$, **$D_g = R_f = \langle -\infty, 20\rangle$** and **$R_g = D_f = \langle e^{-2}, \infty\rangle$**.
questions.pitfall: Examiner report note (avg score 33%): reading $D_g = \mathbb{R} \setminus \{20\}$ from the formula $e^{2x/(20-x)}$ instead of restricting to $D_g = R_f = \langle -\infty, 20\rangle$.

questions.title: Spring 2023 Exam · Problem 1
questions.promptMarkdown: Factorise the polynomial $f(x) = x^4 - 7x^2 + 6x$ into factors of the least possible degree.
rubricChecks: Factor out common factor x first: f(x) = x(x^3 - 7x + 6)
Identify integer zero x = 1 (or 2, -3) of x^3 - 7x + 6 and divide by (x - 1) to get x^2 + x - 6
Factor quadratic x^2 + x - 6 = (x - 2)(x + 3) and state f(x) = x(x - 1)(x - 2)(x + 3)
hints: Hint 1: Always check for a common factor of $x$ first! Factoring out $x$ immediately reduces the degree-$4$ polynomial to $x(x^3 - 7x + 6)$ (Ch. 6).
Hint 2: Test small integer divisors of $6$ ($\pm 1, \pm 2, \pm 3$) in $x^3 - 7x + 6$; remember to leave a $0x^2$ column space during polynomial division!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
First factor out $x$: $f(x) = x(x^3 - 7x + 6)$. Testing $x = 1$ gives $1 - 7 + 6 = 0$, so $(x - 1)$ is a factor. Polynomial division gives:
$$(x^3 + 0x^2 - 7x + 6) : (x - 1) = x^2 + x - 6$$
Factoring $x^2 + x - 6 = (x - 2)(x + 3)$ yields the complete linear factorisation:
$$f(x) = x(x - 1)(x - 2)(x + 3)$$
questions.pitfall: Forgetting the missing $0x^2$ term when dividing $(x^3 - 7x + 6) : (x - 1)$, or dropping the leading factor $x$ in the final answer.

questions.title: Spring 2023 Exam · Problem 2
questions.promptMarkdown:
A hyperbola function $f(x)$ has a horizontal asymptote $y = 100$ and a vertical asymptote $x = 30$. Moreover, $f(40) = 99$.

**i)** Determine the expression for $f(x)$.

**ii)** Draw a sketch of the graph of $f(x)$ with asymptotes.
rubricChecks: Provide a small function value table on both sides of x = 30 (e.g. x = 20, 25, 28, 32, 35, 40)
Sketch both branches accurately with dashed asymptotes x = 30 and y = 100
hints: Hint 1: Substitute $c = 100$, $b = 30$, and $f(40) = 99$ into $f(x) = c + \frac{a}{x - b}$ (Ch. 9).
Hint 2: Note the official guidance explicitly states 'A function table should be provided' — include $2$–$3$ points per branch!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** Using $f(x) = c + \frac{a}{x - b}$ with $c = 100$ and $b = 30$:
$$f(40) = 100 + \frac{a}{40 - 30} = 99 \implies \frac{a}{10} = -1 \implies a = -10$$
Thus **$f(x) = 100 - \dfrac{10}{x - 30}$**.

**ii)** Function table: $(20, 101)$, $(25, 102)$, $(28, 105)$ on the left branch; $(32, 95)$, $(35, 98)$, $(40, 99)$ on the right branch. Sketch both smooth increasing branches approaching dashed asymptotes $x = 30$ and $y = 100$.
questions.pitfall: Sketching the hyperbola freehand without providing a short table of $(x, f(x))$ points, which loses credit per the official grading note.

questions.promptMarkdown:
Calculate the expression for the differentiated function $f'(x)$ if:

**i)** $f(x) = x\sqrt{x}$  
**ii)** $f(x) = \dfrac{3x - 4}{x - 1}$  
**iii)** $f(x) = (2x + 3)^{50} + 11$

Apply quotient rule on (ii): f'(x) = (3(x - 1) - (3x - 4)) / (x - 1)^2 = 1 / (x - 1)^2
Apply chain rule on (iii): f'(x) = 50 * 2 * (2x + 3)^49 = 100(2x + 3)^49
hints: Hint 1: In (i), combine $x \cdot x^{1/2} = x^{3/2}$ before differentiating to avoid a longer product rule (Ch. 2 & 11).
Hint 2: In (iii), remember the inner derivative $u'(x) = 2$ and that the constant $+11$ differentiates to $0$.
questions.pitfall: Forgetting the inner derivative factor $2$ in $(2x+3)^{50}$, writing $50(2x+3)^{49}$ instead of $100(2x+3)^{49}$.

questions.title: Spring 2023 Exam · Problem 4
questions.promptMarkdown:
You are supposed to be paid $2$ million every year for $n$ years with the first payment $5$ years from now. Suppose the interest is $6\%$ with annual compounding.

**i)** Write down the geometric series which gives the present value of the cash flow.

**ii)** Use the geometric series to compute the present value of the cash flow if $n = 20$.

**iii)** Use the geometric series to compute the present value of the cash flow if the payments continue forever.
rubricChecks: Write n-term series starting at 1.06^5 and ending at 1.06^{n+4} (NOT 1.06^{n+5}!)
Evaluate infinite perpetuity sum: (2 / 1.06^5) / (1 - 1/1.06) = 2 / (1.06^4 * 0.06) ≈ 26.40 million
hints: Hint 1: Check the $n=1$ case to avoid fencepost errors! If $n=1$ and the first payment is at year $5$, the last exponent must be $5 = 1 + 4$, so for general $n$ the last exponent is **$n + 4$** (Ch. 4)!
Hint 2: For (ii), read backwards with $n = 20$ ($n + 4 = 24$). For (iii), sum the infinite series with $a_1 = \frac{2}{1.06^5}$ and $k = \frac{1}{1.06}$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** With first payment at $t = 5$ and $n$ annual payments, the $n$-th payment is at $t = n + 4$ (in millions):
$$\frac{2}{1.06^5} + \frac{2}{1.06^6} + \cdots + \frac{2}{1.06^{n+3}} + \frac{2}{1.06^{n+4}}$$

**ii)** Reading backwards ($a_1 = \frac{2}{1.06^{n+4}}$, $k = 1.06$, $n$ terms) at $n = 20$:
$$\text{PV}_{20} = \frac{2}{1.06^{24}} \cdot \frac{1.06^{20} - 1}{0.06} \approx 18.17\text{ million}$$

**iii)** Reading left to right as an infinite geometric series ($a_1 = \frac{2}{1.06^5}$, $k = \frac{1}{1.06}$):
$$\text{PV}_{\infty} = \frac{2}{1.06^5} \cdot \frac{1}{1 - \frac{1}{1.06}} = \frac{2}{1.06^4 \cdot 0.06} \approx 26.40\text{ million}$$
questions.pitfall: Writing last denominator $1.06^{n+5}$ instead of $1.06^{n+4}$ (which gives $n+1$ terms and shifts the $n=20$ value down by $6\%$).

questions.title: Spring 2023 Exam · Problem 5
questions.promptMarkdown:
**i)** Solve the equation $\sqrt{10 - x^2} = x - 2$.

**ii)** Solve the inequality $\ln(x + 2) - \ln(x) \le 0.1$.
rubricChecks: Square sqrt(10 - x^2) = x - 2 to get 2x^2 - 4x - 6 = 0 => x = -1 or x = 3, and reject extraneous x = -1 (where RHS = -3 < 0) so only x = 3
State domain x > 0 for ln(x + 2) - ln(x) <= 0.1 and combine logs to ln((x + 2)/x) <= 0.1 => (x + 2)/x <= e^{0.1}
Solve (1 - e^{0.1})x <= -2 (flipping inequality since 1 - e^{0.1} < 0!) to get x >= 2 / (e^{0.1} - 1) ≈ 19.02
hints: Hint 1: In (i), squaring is only an implication ($\implies$), NOT an equivalence! Check every candidate root back in $\sqrt{10 - x^2} = x - 2$ (requiring $x - 2 \ge 0$, Ch. 1 & 7).
Hint 2: In (ii), note the domain requires $x > 0$, use $\ln(x+2) - \ln(x) = \ln\frac{x+2}{x}$, exponentiate, and watch the sign of $(1 - e^{0.1}) < 0$!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** Squaring both sides gives $10 - x^2 = (x - 2)^2 = x^2 - 4x + 4 \implies 2x^2 - 4x - 6 = 0 \implies x^2 - 2x - 3 = 0$, with candidate roots $x = -1$ and $x = 3$.
- At $x = -1$: LHS $= \sqrt{9} = 3 \ne -3 =$ RHS (extraneous!).
- At $x = 3$: LHS $= \sqrt{1} = 1 = 3 - 2 =$ RHS (valid).
Hence the unique solution is **$x = 3$**.

**ii)** Domain requires $x > 0$ (which also ensures $x + 2 > 0$). Using log rules and the strictly increasing function $e^u$:
$$\ln\!\left(\frac{x + 2}{x}\right) \le 0.1 \iff \frac{x + 2}{x} \le e^{0.1}$$
Since $x > 0$, multiply by $x$: $x + 2 \le e^{0.1}x \iff (e^{0.1} - 1)x \ge 2$. Dividing by $e^{0.1} - 1 > 0$:
$$x \ge \frac{2}{e^{0.1} - 1} \approx 19.02$$
questions.pitfall: Keeping the extraneous root $x = -1$ in (i), or multiplying $\frac{x+2}{x} \le e^{0.1}$ by $x$ without first restricting to the log domain $x > 0$.

questions.title: Spring 2023 Exam · Problem 6
questions.promptMarkdown:
We have a cost function $K(x) = K_0 \cdot e^{0.05x}$ with $x \ge 0$ where $K_0$ is an undetermined positive number.

**i)** Determine the marginal cost function.

**ii)** Calculate the cost optimum and the minimal average unit cost.
rubricChecks: Differentiate K'(x) = 0.05 * K_0 * e^{0.05x} (= 0.05 * K(x))
Solve A(x) = K'(x) => K(x)/x = 0.05*K(x) => 1/x = 0.05 => cost optimum x = 20 (independent of K_0!)
Evaluate minimal average unit cost A(20) = K'(20) = 0.05 * e * K_0 ≈ 0.1359 * K_0
hints: Hint 2: Set $A(x) = \frac{K(x)}{x} = K'(x) = 0.05 K(x)$; since $K(x) > 0$, divide both sides by $K(x)$!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** Marginal cost is $K'(x) = \mathbf{0.05 K_0 e^{0.05x}} = 0.05 K(x)$.

**ii)** Since $K''(x) = 0.0025 K_0 e^{0.05x} > 0$, cost optimum satisfies $A(x) = K'(x)$:
$$\frac{K(x)}{x} = 0.05 K(x) \implies \frac{1}{x} = 0.05 \implies \mathbf{x = 20}$$
Minimal average unit cost is:
$$A(20) = K'(20) = 0.05 K_0 e^{0.05 \cdot 20} = \mathbf{0.05 e K_0} \approx 0.1359 K_0$$
questions.pitfall: Thinking you cannot find a numerical cost optimum $x = 20$ because $K_0$ is unknown ($K_0$ cancels completely out of $A(x) = K'(x)$!).

questions.title: Spring 2023 Exam · Problem 7
questions.promptMarkdown:
We have the function $f(x) = 8x^2 - 25 \cdot \ln(x)$.

**i)** Determine where $f(x)$ is increasing and where it is decreasing.

**ii)** Determine where $f(x)$ is concave and where it is convex.
rubricChecks: State natural domain x > 0 and compute f'(x) = 16x - 25/x = (16x^2 - 25)/x
Restrict stationary points to x > 0 (rejecting -5/4): decreasing on <0, 5/4] and increasing on [5/4, inf>
Compute f''(x) = 16 + 25/x^2 = (16x^2 + 25)/x^2 > 0 for all x > 0: convex on <0, inf> (nowhere concave)
hints: Hint 1: Write down the natural domain of $\ln(x)$ (**$x > 0$**) BEFORE solving any derivative equations (Ch. 10, 12 & 14)!
Hint 2: Differentiate $f'(x) = 16x - 25x^{-1}$ once more to get $f''(x) = 16 + 25x^{-2}$ — watch the sign of $(-25)(-1)$!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
The natural domain of $f(x)$ is $D_f = \langle 0, \infty\rangle$ ($x > 0$).

**i)** $f'(x) = 16x - \frac{25}{x} = \frac{16x^2 - 25}{x} = \frac{(4x - 5)(4x + 5)}{x}$. On $x > 0$, both $x > 0$ and $4x + 5 > 0$, so $f'(x) \le 0$ for $0 < x \le \frac{5}{4}$ and $f'(x) \ge 0$ for $x \ge \frac{5}{4}$. Thus $f(x)$ is **decreasing on $\langle 0, \frac{5}{4}]$** and **increasing on $[\frac{5}{4}, \infty\rangle$**.

**ii)** $f''(x) = 16 + \frac{25}{x^2} = \frac{16x^2 + 25}{x^2} > 0$ for all $x > 0$. Hence $f(x)$ is **convex for all $x > 0$** (and nowhere concave).
questions.pitfall: Including negative values $x \in [-\frac{5}{4}, 0\rangle$ where $\ln(x)$ is undefined, or writing $f''(x) = 16 - \frac{25}{x^2}$ (sign error on $(-x^{-1})' = +x^{-2}$).

questions.title: Spring 2023 Exam · Problem 8
questions.promptMarkdown:
In Figure 1 you see the graph of the function $f(x)$. Determine whether each statement is **true** or **false** and give a short explanation.

**i)** $f(x)$ has three stationary points in the interval $[3, 10]$.

**ii)** $f(x)$ has three inflection points in the interval $\langle 4, 24]$.

**iii)** $f'(x)$ is decreasing in the interval $[12, 24]$.
rubricChecks: Conclude (i) FALSE because horizontal tangents in [3, 10] occur only at x ≈ 4.8 and x ≈ 7.5 (the trough at x ≈ 2.6 is < 3)
Conclude (ii) TRUE because curvature changes sign three times in <4, 24]: x ≈ 6, x ≈ 9.8, and x ≈ 17.8
Conclude (iii) FALSE because f'(x) decreases only where f''(x) <= 0 (concave), and f becomes convex after x ≈ 17.6
hints: Hint 1: Check the left endpoint $x = 3$ carefully in (i): the deep trough near $x \approx 2.6$ lies to the left of $x = 3$ (Ch. 12)!
Hint 2: For (iii), remember $f'(x)$ is decreasing where $(f'(x))' = f''(x) \le 0$, i.e. where $f(x)$ is **concave** (not where $f(x)$ itself is decreasing, Ch. 14)!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i) FALSE.** Stationary points have horizontal tangents ($f'(x) = 0$). Inside $[3, 10]$ this occurs only twice: at $x \approx 4.8$ and $x \approx 7.5$ (the minimum at $x \approx 2.6$ is outside $[3, 10]$).

**ii) TRUE.** Inflection points occur where $f''(x)$ changes sign (between concave and convex). In $\langle 4, 24]$ there are three: $x \approx 6$ (concave $\to$ convex), $x \approx 9.8$ (convex $\to$ concave), and $x \approx 17.8$ (concave $\to$ convex).

**iii) FALSE.** $f'(x)$ is decreasing where $f''(x) \le 0$ ($f$ is concave). On $[12, 24]$, $f(x)$ is concave up to $x \approx 17.6$ and then **convex** ($f'(x)$ increasing) on $[17.6, 24]$.
questions.pitfall: Confusing '$f'(x)$ is decreasing' ($f$ concave) with '$f(x)$ is decreasing' ($f' < 0$) on $[14.2, 24]$.

questions.title: Spring 2023 Exam · Problem 9
questions.promptMarkdown:
Let $p$ be the price of a commodity and suppose $D(p) = 30p^{-0.8}$ with $p > 0$ is the demand function. Let $\varepsilon(p)$ be the momentary price elasticity of the demand function.

**i)** Calculate $\varepsilon(p)$.

**ii)** Determine whether the revenue is going up or down if the price is increasing a little from $p = 20$.
rubricChecks: Apply power rule D'(p) = 30(-0.8)p^{-1.8} and simplify epsilon(p) = -0.8 (constant elasticity)
Note epsilon(20) = -0.8 > -1 (inelastic) and conclude revenue goes UP when price increases from p = 20
hints: Hint 1: Apply the power rule $(p^{-0.8})' = -0.8p^{-1.8}$ and combine exponents $p^{-1.8} \cdot p^1 = p^{-0.8}$ in $\varepsilon(p) = \frac{D'(p)p}{D(p)}$ (Ch. 17).
Hint 2: Compare $\varepsilon(20) = -0.8$ with $-1$ (or inspect $R(p) = pD(p) = 30p^{0.2}$ directly!).
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** By the power rule, $D'(p) = 30(-0.8)p^{-1.8}$, so:
$$\varepsilon(p) = \frac{30(-0.8)p^{-1.8} \cdot p}{30p^{-0.8}} = -0.8$$
(a constant-elasticity isoelastic demand function).

**ii)** Since $\varepsilon(20) = -0.8 > -1$, demand is **inelastic** at $p = 20$, so **revenue goes up** if the price increases slightly from $20$ (confirmed directly by $R(p) = pD(p) = 30p^{0.2}$, which is strictly increasing).
questions.pitfall: Subtracting $-0.8 - 1 = -0.2$ instead of $-1.8$ when differentiating $p^{-0.8}$, or confusing $-0.8 > -1$ (inelastic) with elastic.

questions.title: Spring 2023 Exam · Problem 10
questions.promptMarkdown:
We have the function $f(x) = e^{-0.02x} + 100$ with domain of definition $D_f = [0, \infty\rangle$. Let $g(x)$ be the inverse function of $f(x)$.

**i)** Determine the expression of $g(x)$.

**ii)** Determine the domain of definition $D_g$ and the range $R_g$ of $g(x)$.
rubricChecks: Solve y = e^{-0.02x} + 100 for x to get g(x) = -50 * ln(x - 100)
Determine D_g = R_f = <100, 101] using decreasing monotonicity, f(0) = 101, and lim_{x->inf} f(x) = 100+
State R_g = D_f = [0, inf>
hints: Hint 1: Subtract $100$ from both sides of $y = e^{-0.02x} + 100$, apply $\ln$, and divide by $-0.02 = -\frac{1}{50}$ (Ch. 10).
Hint 2: Remember $D_g = R_f$: evaluate $f(0)$ and $\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x)$ on $D_f = [0, \infty\rangle$!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** From $y = e^{-0.02x} + 100$: $e^{-0.02x} = y - 100 \implies -0.02x = \ln(y - 100) \implies x = -50\ln(y - 100)$. Swapping variables:
$$g(x) = -50\ln(x - 100)$$

**ii)** Since $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing on $D_f = [0, \infty\rangle$ with $f(0) = 1 + 100 = 101$ and $\lim_{x \to \infty} (e^{-0.02x} + 100) = 100^+$, we get:
$$D_g = R_f = \langle 100, 101], \qquad R_g = D_f = [0, \infty\rangle$$
questions.pitfall: Writing $D_g = \langle 100, \infty\rangle$ from $x - 100 > 0$ instead of restricting to $R_f = \langle 100, 101]$.

questions.title: Spring 2023 Exam · Problem 11
questions.promptMarkdown:
**i)** A bank account has $7.2\%$ nominal interest and continuous compounding. Determine the effective interest.

**ii)** Suppose $A$ and $B$ are two undetermined positive numbers. An investment of $A$ million is supposed to give a payment of $B$ million $5$ years from now. Determine the internal rate of return for the cash flow.
rubricChecks: Compute effective annual rate r_eff = e^{0.072} - 1 ≈ 7.47%
Set up NPV = -A + B / (1 + r)^5 = 0 and solve symbolic IRR r = (B / A)^{1/5} - 1 (or (1/5) ln(B/A) under continuous compounding)
hints: Hint 1: Under continuous compounding at nominal rate $r$, the $1$-year growth factor is $e^r = 1 + r_{\text{eff}}$ (Ch. 2 & 4).
Hint 2: In (ii), solve $-A + \frac{B}{(1+r)^5} = 0$ for $r$ in terms of $A$ and $B$ (Ch. 3).
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** With continuous compounding at $r = 0.072$, the annual growth factor is $e^{0.072}$, so the effective annual interest rate is:
$$r_{\text{eff}} = e^{0.072} - 1 \approx 0.074655 = \mathbf{7.47\%}$$

**ii)** With standard annual compounding, $\text{NPV} = -A + \frac{B}{(1 + r)^5} = 0 \implies (1 + r)^5 = \frac{B}{A}$, giving:
$$r = \left(\frac{B}{A}\right)^{\frac{1}{5}} - 1$$
*(Note: if continuous compounding is assumed instead, $-A + Be^{-5r} = 0 \implies r = \frac{1}{5}\ln(B/A)$ — both receive full credit in the official key.)*
questions.pitfall: Writing $(A/B)^{1/5} - 1$ (inverting outflow and inflow) or forgetting to subtract $1$ from the growth factor.

questions.title: Spring 2023 Exam · Problem 12
questions.promptMarkdown:
We have a curve implicitly given by the equation $x^3 - 4xy + y^2 = -2$.

**i)** Find an expression for $y'$ in terms of $y$ and $x$.

**ii)** Determine the expression for the tangent of the curve at the point $(1, 3)$.
rubricChecks: Differentiate implicitly: 3x^2 - 4y - 4xy' + 2yy' = 0 => y' = (4y - 3x^2) / (2y - 4x)
Write tangent line equation y - 3 = 4.5(x - 1) => y = 4.5x - 1.5
hints: Hint 1: Differentiate $x^3 - 4xy + y^2 = -2$ implicitly with respect to $x$; remember the constant $-2$ differentiates to $0$ (Ch. 13).
Hint 2: Evaluate slope $a = y'(1, 3)$ and substitute into the point-slope formula $y - y_0 = a(x - x_0)$ (Ch. 8 & 11).
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** Differentiating both sides with respect to $x$:
$$3x^2 - 4y - 4xy' + 2yy' = 0 \implies (2y - 4x)y' = 4y - 3x^2 \implies y' = \frac{4y - 3x^2}{2y - 4x}$$

**ii)** At $(1, 3)$, the slope is $a = \frac{4(3) - 3(1)^2}{2(3) - 4(1)} = \frac{9}{2} = 4.5$. Using the point-slope formula:
$$y - 3 = 4.5(x - 1) \implies \mathbf{y = 4.5x - 1.5}$$
questions.pitfall: Stopping after computing the slope $4.5$ when part (ii) asks for the **expression for the tangent** line $y = 4.5x - 1.5$.

questions.title: Autumn 2022 Exam · Problem 2
questions.promptMarkdown: Factorise the polynomial $f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 3x + 1$ into factors of the least possible degree.
rubricChecks: Test divisors ±1 of constant term 1 to find f(-1) = -1 - 3 + 3 + 1 = 0 => (x + 1) is a factor
Perform polynomial division (x^3 - 3x^2 - 3x + 1) : (x + 1) = x^2 - 4x + 1
Find irrational roots 2 ± sqrt(3) of x^2 - 4x + 1 = 0 and write (x + 1)(x - 2 + sqrt(3))(x - 2 - sqrt(3))
hints: Hint 1: Any integer zero must divide the constant term $1$ ($x = \pm 1$). Test $f(1)$ and $f(-1)$ first (Ch. 6)!
Hint 2: After dividing by $(x + 1)$ to get $x^2 - 4x + 1$, don't stop just because it has no integer roots — solve $x^2 - 4x + 1 = 0$ using completing the square or the quadratic formula!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Testing divisors of $1$: $f(-1) = (-1)^3 - 3(-1)^2 - 3(-1) + 1 = -1 - 3 + 3 + 1 = 0$, so $(x + 1)$ is a factor. Polynomial division gives:
$$(x^3 - 3x^2 - 3x + 1) : (x + 1) = x^2 - 4x + 1$$
Solving $x^2 - 4x + 1 = 0 \iff (x - 2)^2 = 3 \iff x = 2 \pm \sqrt{3}$ gives the complete linear factorisation:
$$f(x) = (x + 1)(x - 2 + \sqrt{3})(x - 2 - \sqrt{3})$$
questions.pitfall: Examiner report trap (avg score 41%): stopping at $(x + 1)(x^2 - 4x + 1)$ because $x^2 - 4x + 1$ has no *integer* roots, overlooking its two real irrational roots $2 \pm \sqrt{3}$!

questions.title: Autumn 2022 Exam · Problem 3
questions.promptMarkdown: Calculate the limit $\lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{0.5x + 1 - \sqrt{x + 1}}{x^2}$.
rubricChecks: Verify 0/0 indeterminate form at x = 0 and apply first L'Hôpital step to get lim_{x->0} (0.5 - 1/(2*sqrt(x+1))) / (2x)
Verify the resulting limit is STILL 0/0 at x = 0 and apply L'Hôpital's rule a second time
hints: Hint 1: Check that $x = 0$ gives $\frac{0}{0}$ and apply L'Hôpital's rule once: $(0.5x + 1 - (x+1)^{1/2})' = 0.5 - \frac{1}{2}(x+1)^{-1/2}$ (Ch. 15).
Hint 2: Check $x = 0$ again after the first step — it is **still** $\frac{0}{0}$, so apply L'Hôpital's rule a second time watching $-\frac{1}{2} \cdot (-\frac{1}{2}) = +\frac{1}{4}$!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
At $x = 0$, the expression is $\frac{1 - 1}{0} = \frac{0}{0}$. Applying L'Hôpital's rule once:
$$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{0.5x + 1 - \sqrt{x + 1}}{x^2} \stackrel{\text{L'H}}{=} \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{0.5 - \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x + 1}}}{2x}$$
This is again $\frac{0.5 - 0.5}{0} = \frac{0}{0}$. Applying L'Hôpital's rule a second time (with $(-\frac{1}{2}(x+1)^{-1/2})' = +\frac{1}{4}(x+1)^{-3/2}$):
$$\stackrel{\text{L'H}}{=} \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\frac{1}{4(x + 1)\sqrt{x + 1}}}{2} = \frac{\frac{1}{4}}{2} = \mathbf{\frac{1}{8}}$$
questions.pitfall: Examiner report note (avg score 47%): sign or power error when differentiating $-\frac{1}{2}(x+1)^{-1/2}$, giving $-\frac{1}{8}$ or $\frac{1}{4}$ instead of $+\frac{1}{8}$.

questions.title: Autumn 2022 Exam · Problem 4
questions.promptMarkdown:
**i)** A bank account has $3.6\%$ nominal interest with monthly compounding. Determine the effective interest.

**ii)** An investment of $15$ million is supposed to give a payment of $30$ million $6$ years from now. Determine the internal rate of return.
rubricChecks: Compute monthly rate 3.6% / 12 = 0.3% and effective annual interest (1.003)^12 - 1 ≈ 3.66%
hints: Hint 1: Divide nominal $3.6\%$ by $12$ to get $0.3\%$ per month, compound $12$ times, and subtract $1$ (Ch. 2).
Hint 2: For (ii), set $\text{NPV} = -15 + \frac{30}{(1+r)^6} = 0$ and solve $(1+r)^6 = 2$ (Ch. 3).
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** Monthly interest rate is $\frac{3.6\%}{12} = 0.3\% = 0.003$. Annual growth factor is $1.003^{12} \approx 1.0366$, giving effective interest **$3.66\%$**.

**ii)** Setting $\text{NPV} = -15 + \frac{30}{(1 + r)^6} = 0$ gives $(1 + r)^6 = \frac{30}{15} = 2$, so:
$$r = 2^{\frac{1}{6}} - 1 \approx 0.12246 = \mathbf{12.25\%}$$
questions.pitfall: Examiner report note (avg score 42%): rounding $1.003^{12}$ too early to $1.04$ ($4\%$) instead of keeping two decimal places ($3.66\%$).

questions.title: Autumn 2022 Exam · Problem 5
questions.promptMarkdown: Show that the function $f(x) = 0.03x^2 + 5x + 200 + 300e^{0.01x}$ is a cost function.
rubricChecks: Verify positive fixed cost at x = 0: f(0) = 200 + 300 = 500 > 0
Verify increasing for x >= 0: f'(x) = 0.06x + 5 + 3e^{0.01x} >= 8 > 0 for all x >= 0
Verify convex for x >= 0: f''(x) = 0.06 + 0.03e^{0.01x} >= 0.09 > 0 for all x >= 0
hints: Hint 1: Recall the **three mathematical conditions** defining a standard BI cost function on $x \ge 0$: (1) $f(0) > 0$, (2) $f$ increasing ($f'(x) \ge 0$), and (3) $f$ convex ($f''(x) \ge 0$, Ch. 16)!
Hint 2: Explicitly compute $f(0)$, $f'(x)$, and $f''(x)$, and explain why each is $\ge 0$ (or $> 0$) for all $x \ge 0$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Check the three cost-function conditions on $x \ge 0$:
1. **Positive fixed cost:** $f(0) = 0 + 0 + 200 + 300e^0 = 500 > 0$.
2. **Increasing ($f'(x) \ge 0$):** $f'(x) = 0.06x + 5 + 3e^{0.01x} \ge 0 + 5 + 3 = 8 > 0$ for all $x \ge 0$.
3. **Convex ($f''(x) \ge 0$):** $f''(x) = 0.06 + 0.03e^{0.01x} \ge 0.06 + 0.03 = 0.09 > 0$ for all $x \ge 0$.

Since all three conditions hold for $x \ge 0$, $f(x)$ is a cost function.
questions.pitfall: Examiner report note (avg score 42%): checking only $f'(x) > 0$ and forgetting either $f(0) > 0$ (remember $e^0 = 1$, so $f(0) = 500$, not $200$!) or convexity $f''(x) \ge 0$.

questions.title: Autumn 2022 Exam · Problem 6
questions.promptMarkdown:
Let $p$ be the price of a commodity and assume $D(p) = (p + 20)e^{-0.05p}$ with $p > 0$ is the demand function. Let $\varepsilon(p)$ be the momentary price elasticity of the demand function.

**i)** Calculate $\varepsilon(p)$.

**ii)** Determine whether the revenue is going up or down if the price is increasing a little from $p = 40$.
rubricChecks: Simplify epsilon(p) = D'(p)*p / D(p) = -0.05p^2 / (p + 20)
Evaluate epsilon(40) = -80 / 60 = -4/3 < -1 (elastic) and conclude revenue goes down when price rises slightly from 40
hints: Hint 1: Use **both** the product rule and chain rule on $D(p) = (p + 20)e^{-0.05p}$, then factor out $e^{-0.05p}$ before forming $\varepsilon(p)$ (Ch. 11 & 17)!
Hint 2: Notice $1 - 0.05(p + 20) = 1 - 0.05p - 1 = -0.05p$ simplifies cleanly! Then evaluate $\varepsilon(40)$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** By the product and chain rules:
$$D'(p) = 1 \cdot e^{-0.05p} + (p + 20)(-0.05e^{-0.05p}) = (1 - 0.05p - 1)e^{-0.05p} = -0.05pe^{-0.05p}$$
Hence:
$$\varepsilon(p) = \frac{D'(p) \cdot p}{D(p)} = \frac{-0.05p^2 e^{-0.05p}}{(p + 20)e^{-0.05p}} = \frac{-0.05p^2}{p + 20}$$

**ii)** At $p = 40$, $\varepsilon(40) = \frac{-0.05 \cdot 1600}{60} = -\frac{80}{60} = -\frac{4}{3} < -1$. Demand is price elastic at $p = 40$, so **revenue decreases** if the price increases slightly from $40$.
questions.pitfall: Examiner report note (lowest score on first two pages, avg 33%!): forgetting the product rule on $(p + 20)e^{-0.05p}$.

questions.title: Autumn 2022 Exam · Problem 8
questions.promptMarkdown:
In Figure 2 you see the graph of **$f'(x)$**. Determine whether each statement is **true** or **false** and give a short explanation.

**i)** $f(x)$ has three stationary points.

**ii)** $f(4) > f(8)$.

**iii)** $f(x)$ has three inflection points.
rubricChecks: Conclude (i) FALSE because f'(x) = 0 crosses the x-axis FOUR times (x ≈ 1.3, 3.0, 8.2, and 12.7)
Conclude (ii) FALSE because f'(x) > 0 on <4, 8>, so f(x) is strictly increasing on [4, 8] and f(4) < f(8)
Conclude (iii) TRUE because f''(x) changes sign at the three local extrema of f'(x) (x ≈ 1.9, 4.9, and 10.1)
hints: Hint 1: The plotted graph is **$f'(x)$**! Scan the entire horizontal axis from $x=1$ to $x=13$ so you don't miss the fourth zero near $x \approx 12.7$ (Ch. 12).
Hint 2: On $[4, 8]$, $f'(x)$ is decreasing in height, **but it is strictly positive** ($f'(x) > 0$)! What does $f'(x) > 0$ say about $f(4)$ vs $f(8)$?
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i) FALSE.** Stationary points of $f(x)$ satisfy $f'(x) = 0$. The graph of $f'(x)$ crosses the $x$-axis **four** times: $x \approx 1.3$, $x \approx 3.0$, $x \approx 8.2$, and $x \approx 12.7$.

**ii) FALSE.** Because $f'(x) > 0$ throughout $\langle 4, 8\rangle$, $f(x)$ is strictly increasing on $[4, 8]$, so $f(4) < f(8)$.

**iii) TRUE.** Inflection points of $f(x)$ occur where $f''(x)$ changes sign, i.e. at local maxima and minima of $f'(x)$, of which there are **three** ($x \approx 1.9$, $x \approx 4.9$, and $x \approx 10.1$).
questions.pitfall: Seeing $f'(4) \approx 2.8 > 0.2 \approx f'(8)$ and concluding $f(4) > f(8)$ in (ii), or overlooking the rightmost $x$-intercept near $x = 12.7$ in (i).

questions.title: Autumn 2022 Exam · Problem 9
questions.promptMarkdown:
We have the function $f(x) = 5\ln(x^2 - 20x + 102)$ with domain of definition $D_f = [0, 25]$.

**i)** Determine the minimum point and the maximum point of $f(x)$.

**ii)** Determine the maximum and minimum of $f(x)$.
rubricChecks: Verify inner quadratic x^2 - 20x + 102 = (x - 10)^2 + 2 >= 2 > 0 and compute f'(x) = 5(2x - 20) / (x^2 - 20x + 102)
Find unique stationary point x = 10 and compare f(0) = 5 ln(102) ≈ 23.12, f(10) = 5 ln(2) ≈ 3.47, and f(25) = 5 ln(227) ≈ 27.12
Distinguish points (min point x = 10, max point x = 25) in (i) from values (min 5 ln 2 ≈ 3.47, max 5 ln 227 ≈ 27.12) in (ii)
hints: Hint 1: Differentiate using the chain rule (or notice $\ln(u)$ is strictly increasing, so extrema of $f$ match extrema of $u(x) = (x - 10)^2 + 2$ on $[0, 25]$, Ch. 10 & 12)!
Hint 2: Know BI's terminology! **Minimum/maximum point** means the **$x$-value** ($x = 10$, $x = 25$), whereas **minimum/maximum** means the **function value** $f(x)$!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** Since $u(x) = x^2 - 20x + 102 = (x - 10)^2 + 2 \ge 2 > 0$, $f$ is smooth on $[0, 25]$ with:
$$f'(x) = \frac{5(2x - 20)}{x^2 - 20x + 102} = 0 \iff x = 10$$
Comparing the stationary point and both endpoints of $[0, 25]$:
- $f(0) = 5\ln(102) \approx 23.12$
- $f(10) = 5\ln(2) \approx 3.47$
- $f(25) = 5\ln(25^2 - 500 + 102) = 5\ln(227) \approx 27.12$

Thus **$x = 10$ is the minimum point** and **$x = 25$ is the maximum point**.

**ii)** The **minimum value is $f(10) = 5\ln(2) \approx 3.47$** and the **maximum value is $f(25) = 5\ln(227) \approx 27.12$**.
questions.pitfall: Examiner report note (avg score 52%): confusing 'maximum point' ($x = 25$) with 'maximum' ($f(25) = 27.12$), or forgetting to test the endpoints $x = 0$ and $x = 25$.

**ii)** Determine the expression of the inverse function $g(x)$.
rubricChecks: Show f(x) = 2022 - 2022/(e^x + 1) (or f'(x) = 2022e^x/(e^x + 1)^2 > 0) is strictly increasing with limits 0 (as x -> -inf) and 2022 (as x -> +inf)
State D_g = R_f = <0, 2022> and R_g = D_f = R (whole number line)
Solve y = 2022e^x / (e^x + 1) for e^x = y / (2022 - y) and write g(x) = ln(x / (2022 - x)) = ln(x) - ln(2022 - x)
hints: Hint 1: Notice part (i) comes **before** part (ii)! Find $D_g = R_f$ by checking monotonicity of $f(x)$ and evaluating $\lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x)$ and $\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x)$ (Ch. 9 & 10).
Hint 2: For (ii), multiply $y = \frac{2022e^x}{e^x + 1}$ by $(e^x + 1)$, group all $e^x$ terms together as $(2022 - y)e^x = y$, and take $\ln$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** Rewrite $f(x) = 2022 - \frac{2022}{e^x + 1}$ (or compute $f'(x) = \frac{2022e^x}{(e^x + 1)^2} > 0$), so $f$ is strictly increasing on $\mathbb{R}$. Since:
$$\lim_{x \to -\infty} \frac{2022e^x}{e^x + 1} = \frac{0}{1} = 0, \qquad \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{2022e^x}{e^x + 1} = \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{2022}{1 + e^{-x}} = 2022$$
we obtain **$D_g = R_f = \langle 0, 2022\rangle$** and **$R_g = D_f = \mathbb{R}$** (the whole number line).

**ii)** Solving $y = \frac{2022e^x}{e^x + 1}$ for $x$: $ye^x + y = 2022e^x \implies (2022 - y)e^x = y \implies e^x = \frac{y}{2022 - y}$. Since $y \in \langle 0, 2022\rangle$, $\frac{y}{2022 - y} > 0$, giving:
$$g(x) = \ln\!\left(\frac{x}{2022 - x}\right) = \ln(x) - \ln(2022 - x)$$
questions.pitfall: Examiner report note (lowest score on 2022H, avg 30%!): failing to isolate $e^x$ when it appears in both numerator and denominator, or including $0$ or $2022$ in $D_g$.

questions.title: Autumn 2022 Exam · Problem 12
questions.promptMarkdown:
**i)** The price of a commodity changes from $a$ kroner to $b$ kroner. Determine the relative change.

**ii)** The price of a commodity changes three times with relative changes $r_1$, $r_2$ and $r_3$. After these price changes the commodity costs $b$ kroner. What was its cost before these three price changes?
rubricChecks: State relative change formula (new - old) / old = (b - a) / a
Compound three growth factors a * (1 + r_1)(1 + r_2)(1 + r_3) = b
Solve initial cost a = b / ((1 + r_1)(1 + r_2)(1 + r_3))
hints: Hint 1: Relative change is always measured relative to the **initial (old)** value $a$: $\frac{\text{new} - \text{old}}{\text{old}}$ (Ch. 2).
Hint 2: Each relative change $r_i$ multiplies the price by growth factor $(1 + r_i)$ — never add $r_1 + r_2 + r_3$!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**i)** Relative change is:
$$\frac{\text{new price} - \text{old price}}{\text{old price}} = \frac{b - a}{a} \quad \left(= \frac{b}{a} - 1\right)$$

**ii)** Let $a$ be the initial price. Successive relative changes $r_1, r_2, r_3$ multiply by $(1 + r_1)(1 + r_2)(1 + r_3)$:
$$a(1 + r_1)(1 + r_2)(1 + r_3) = b \implies a = \frac{b}{(1 + r_1)(1 + r_2)(1 + r_3)}$$
questions.pitfall: Examiner report trap (avg score 34%!): writing $\frac{b}{1 + r_1 + r_2 + r_3}$ or $b(1 - r_1)(1 - r_2)(1 - r_3)$ instead of dividing by the product of growth factors $(1 + r_1)(1 + r_2)(1 + r_3)$.

questions.title: Autumn 2022 Course Paper 1 · Problem 1
questions.promptMarkdown:
**a)** Calculate the sum
$$25\,000 \cdot 1.004^{276} + 25\,000 \cdot 1.004^{274} + 25\,000 \cdot 1.004^{272} + \cdots + 25\,000 \cdot 1.004^{38}$$

**b)** Describe a financial situation where this sum is relevant (the important numbers should be interpreted).
rubricChecks: Read backwards with first term a1 = 25,000 * 1.004^38 and common ratio k = 1.004^2
Count exact number of even-exponent terms n = (276 - 38)/2 + 1 = 120
Evaluate sum = 25,000 * 1.004^38 * (1.004^240 - 1) / (1.004^2 - 1) ≈ 5,831,740.85 and interpret 4.8% nominal monthly compounding with 120 bi-monthly deposits over 23 years
hints: Hint 1: Notice the exponents step by $2$ ($38, 40, \dots, 276$), so read from right to left with ratio $k = 1.004^2$ (Ch. 4).
Hint 2: Count terms carefully via $\frac{276 - 38}{2} + 1 = 120$. For (b), $0.4\%$ per month corresponds to $12 \cdot 0.4\% = 4.8\%$ nominal annual interest with monthly compounding.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**a)** Reading from right to left gives a geometric series with $a_1 = 25\,000 \cdot 1.004^{38}$, multiplication factor $k = 1.004^2$, and $n = \frac{276 - 38}{2} + 1 = 120$ terms:
$$S = 25\,000 \cdot 1.004^{38} \cdot \frac{(1.004^2)^{120} - 1}{1.004^2 - 1} = 25\,000 \cdot 1.004^{38} \cdot \frac{1.004^{240} - 1}{1.004^2 - 1} \approx 5\,831\,740.85$$

**b)** Account balance **$23$ years ($276$ months)** from now at **$4.8\%$ nominal annual interest with monthly compounding** ($0.4\%$ per month), where **$25\,000$ is deposited every second month** ($120$ deposits in total), starting today, with the last deposit after $19$ years and $10$ months ($238$ months) so the final deposit earns interest for the remaining $38$ months ($3$ years and $2$ months).
questions.pitfall: Using $n = 276 - 38 + 1 = 239$ instead of dividing the exponent step by $2$ ($n = 120$), or dividing by $0.004$ instead of $1.004^2 - 1 = 0.008016$.

questions.title: Autumn 2022 Course Paper 1 · Problem 2
questions.promptMarkdown:
Consider the cash flow with continuous compounding and nominal annual interest $r$:

| Year | $4$ | $6$ | $9$ |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Payment | $A$ | $B$ | $C$ |

**a)** Write down an expression for the present value of the cash flow, and calculate it when $A = 20$, $B = 30$, $C = 50$ and $r = 10\%$.

**b)** Write down an expression for the future value of the cash flow in year $7$, and calculate it with the numbers from (a).

**c)** With $A = 20$, $B = 30$, $C = 50$: **i)** determine $r$ such that the present values of $A$ and $B$ are equal; **ii)** determine $r$ such that the present value of $C$ is greater than the present value of $B$.

**d)** Determine for which $r$ the ordering of present values is $\text{PV}(A) < \text{PV}(C) < \text{PV}(B)$.
rubricChecks: Combine pairwise inequalities in (d) to obtain (ln 5 - ln 3)/3 < r < (ln 5 - ln 2)/5 (17.03% < r < 18.33%)
hints: Hint 1: Under continuous compounding at nominal rate $r$, discounting $t$ years multiplies by $e^{-rt}$, and moving from $t = 0$ to year $7$ multiplies by $e^{7r}$ (Ch. 3 & 4).
Hint 2: For (c)–(d), compare pairs by isolating the exponential: e.g. $20e^{-4r} < 50e^{-9r} \iff e^{5r} < \frac{5}{2} \iff r < \frac{\ln 5 - \ln 2}{5}$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**a)** $\text{PV} = Ae^{-4r} + Be^{-6r} + Ce^{-9r}$. For $A=20, B=30, C=50, r=0.10$:
$$\text{PV} = 20e^{-0.4} + 30e^{-0.6} + 50e^{-0.9} \approx 50.20$$

**b)** $\text{FV}_7 = \text{PV} \cdot e^{7r} = Ae^{3r} + Be^{r} + Ce^{-2r} \approx 50.2016 \cdot e^{0.7} \approx \mathbf{101.09}$.

**c) i)** $20e^{-4r} = 30e^{-6r} \iff e^{2r} = \frac{3}{2} \iff r = \frac{\ln 3 - \ln 2}{2} \approx \mathbf{20.27\%}$.
**ii)** $50e^{-9r} > 30e^{-6r} \iff e^{3r} < \frac{5}{3} \iff r < \frac{\ln 5 - \ln 3}{3} \approx \mathbf{17.03\%}$.

**d)** We need both $\text{PV}(C) < \text{PV}(B)$ (which by c-ii holds iff $r > \frac{\ln 5 - \ln 3}{3} \approx 17.03\%$) and $\text{PV}(A) < \text{PV}(C)$:
$$20e^{-4r} < 50e^{-9r} \iff e^{5r} < 2.5 \iff r < \frac{\ln 5 - \ln 2}{5} \approx 18.33\%$$
(Notice this automatically implies $\text{PV}(A) < \text{PV}(B)$ since $18.33\% < 20.27\%$.) Hence **$\frac{\ln 5 - \ln 3}{3} < r < \frac{\ln 5 - \ln 2}{5}$** ($17.03\% < r < 18.33\%$).
questions.pitfall: Forgetting that $C$ at year $9$ is still $2$ years in the future when computing $\text{FV}_7$, so its exponent in $\text{FV}_7$ is $-2r$, not $+2r$.

questions.title: Autumn 2022 Course Paper 1 · Problem 4
questions.promptMarkdown:
**a)** Solve the equation $\sqrt{4x + 9} = x + 1$.

**b)** Determine the values of the parameter $t$ such that the equation $\sqrt{4x + 9} = x + t$ has **no** solutions.

**c)** Determine the values of the parameter $k$ such that the equation $x^4 + 6x^2 = k$ has solutions.
rubricChecks: Square sqrt(4x + 9) = x + 1 to get x^2 - 2x - 8 = 0 => x = 4 or x = -2, and reject extraneous x = -2 so x = 4
Square sqrt(4x + 9) = x + t to x^2 + 2(t - 2)x + (t^2 - 9) = 0, find discriminant -16t + 52 < 0 <=> t > 3.25 (and verify for t <= 3.25 the larger root satisfies x + t >= 0)
Substitute u = x^2 >= 0 in u^2 + 6u = k: (u + 3)^2 = k + 9 gives u = -3 + sqrt(k + 9) >= 0 <=> k >= 0
hints: Hint 1: Squaring $\sqrt{4x + 9} = x + t$ is only an implication ($\Rightarrow$), so always test candidate roots against $x + t \ge 0$ (Ch. 1, 5 & 7).

Hint 2: In (b), check both when the quadratic $x^2 + (2t - 4)x + t^2 - 9 = 0$ has negative discriminant AND whether at least one root satisfies $x + t \ge 0$ when $\Delta \ge 0$. In (c), note $x^4 + 6x^2 \ge 0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**a)** Squaring gives $4x + 9 = (x + 1)^2 = x^2 + 2x + 1 \implies x^2 - 2x - 8 = 0 \implies (x - 4)(x + 2) = 0$.
- $x = 4$: LHS $= \sqrt{25} = 5$, RHS $= 5$ (valid).
- $x = -2$: LHS $= \sqrt{1} = 1 \ne -1 =$ RHS (extraneous). Unique solution: **$x = 4$**.

**b)** Squaring $\sqrt{4x + 9} = x + t$ yields $x^2 + 2(t - 2)x + t^2 - 9 = 0$, or $(x + t - 2)^2 = 13 - 4t$.
- If $13 - 4t < 0 \iff t > \frac{13}{4} = 3.25$, even the squared equation has no real roots.
- If $t \le 3.25$, the larger root is $x = 2 - t + \sqrt{13 - 4t}$, for which $x + t = 2 + \sqrt{13 - 4t} \ge 2 > 0$, so it always solves the original radical equation!
Hence the equation has **no solutions iff $t > 3.25$** ($t > \frac{13}{4}$).

**c)** Let $u = x^2 \ge 0$. Completing the square on $u^2 + 6u = k$ gives $(u + 3)^2 = k + 9$. We need $k + 9 \ge 0$ and the larger root $u = -3 + \sqrt{k + 9} \ge 0 \iff \sqrt{k + 9} \ge 3 \iff k + 9 \ge 9 \iff \mathbf{k \ge 0}$.
questions.pitfall: In (c), requiring only positive discriminant $k + 9 \ge 0 \implies k \ge -9$ and forgetting that $u = x^2$ must be **non-negative** ($k \ge 0$).

questions.title: Autumn 2022 Course Paper 1 · Problem 5
questions.promptMarkdown:
Suppose $g(x)$ is a function defined on the whole number line such that $g(x) > 0$ when $x < 3$, $g(3) = 0$, and $g(x) < 0$ when $x > 3$. Solve the inequalities:

**a)** $(x - 1)(x + 2)g(x) \ge 0$  
**b)** $e^{2 - x}\ln(x)g(x) < 0$  
**c)** $\dfrac{(3x - 5)g(x)}{x - 5} \le g(x)$  
**d)** $\dfrac{g(x)^2 + 4}{e^{2x} - 10} > 0$
rubricChecks: Build sign chart in (a) with roots -2, 1, 3 (remembering g(x) goes + to - at 3): x <= -2 or 1 <= x <= 3
Restrict (b) to x > 0 with e^{2-x} > 0, ln(x) zero at 1, g(x) zero at 3: 0 < x < 1 or x > 3
Subtract g(x) in (c) WITHOUT cancelling g(x) to get 2x*g(x)/(x - 5) <= 0 => 0 <= x <= 3 or x > 5
Note g(x)^2 + 4 >= 4 > 0 everywhere in (d), so e^{2x} - 10 > 0 => x > (ln 10)/2
hints: Hint 1: Treat $g(x)$ as a factor in your sign diagram that is $+$ to the left of $3$, $0$ at $3$, and $-$ to the right of $3$ (just like $(3 - x)$, Ch. 7).
Hint 2: In (c), **never divide by $g(x)$ or multiply by $(x - 5)$**! Subtract $g(x)$ to the left and combine over $(x - 5)$: $\frac{(3x - 5 - (x - 5))g(x)}{x - 5} = \frac{2xg(x)}{x - 5} \le 0$.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**a)** Factors $(x + 2)$, $(x - 1)$, and $g(x)$ have zeros at $-2, 1, 3$ (with $g(x) > 0$ for $x < 3$ and $g(x) < 0$ for $x > 3$). Sign diagram gives **$x \le -2$ or $1 \le x \le 3$**.

**b)** Defined only for $x > 0$. Since $e^{2 - x} > 0$ everywhere, sign is determined by $\ln(x)$ (negative on $\langle 0, 1\rangle$, positive on $\langle 1, \infty\rangle$) and $g(x)$: **$0 < x < 1$ or $x > 3$**.

**c)** Move $g(x)$ to the left and combine into a single fraction:
$$\frac{(3x - 5)g(x) - (x - 5)g(x)}{x - 5} = \frac{2x \cdot g(x)}{x - 5} \le 0$$
Sign diagram with $2x$ ($0$ at $0$), $g(x)$ ($0$ at $3$), and $(x - 5)$ (undefined at $5$) gives **$0 \le x \le 3$ or $x > 5$**.

**d)** Since $g(x)^2 \ge 0$, the numerator $g(x)^2 + 4 \ge 4 > 0$ is strictly positive for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$. Thus we need $e^{2x} - 10 > 0 \iff 2x > \ln 10 \iff \mathbf{x > \frac{\ln 10}{2}}$.
questions.pitfall: Dividing both sides of (c) by $g(x)$ — which loses the root $x = 3$ and flips the inequality on $x > 3$ where $g(x) < 0$!

questions.title: Autumn 2022 Course Paper 1 · Problem 6
questions.promptMarkdown:
Let $f(x) = x^3 + bx^2 + cx - 125$ and $g(x) = x - 5$ where $b$ and $c$ are parameters.

**a)** Perform the polynomial division $f(x) : g(x)$.

**b)** Determine the condition on $b$ and $c$ for $g(x)$ to be a factor in $f(x)$.
rubricChecks: Divide (x^3 + bx^2 + cx - 125) : (x - 5) cleanly keeping symbolic coefficients
Obtain quotient x^2 + (b + 5)x + (5b + c + 25) and remainder 25b + 5c
Set remainder 25b + 5c = 0 <=> c = -5b (or 5b + c = 0)
hints: Hint 1: Carry $(b + 5)$ and $(5b + c + 25)$ in parentheses as single coefficients during long division (Ch. 6).
Hint 2: Check your remainder using the Remainder Theorem: $f(5) = 5^3 + 25b + 5c - 125 = 25b + 5c$!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**a)** Performing polynomial long division of $x^3 + bx^2 + cx - 125$ by $x - 5$:
$$\frac{x^3 + bx^2 + cx - 125}{x - 5} = x^2 + (b + 5)x + (25 + 5b + c) + \frac{25b + 5c}{x - 5}$$
(Notice the $-125$ cancels $+5 \cdot 25 = 125$, leaving remainder $25b + 5c$.)

**b)** $x - 5$ is a factor of $f(x)$ iff the remainder is zero:
$$25b + 5c = 0 \iff 5b + c = 0 \iff c = -5b$$
questions.pitfall: Sign mistakes when subtracting $-(b + 5)x(x - 5) = -(b + 5)x^2 + (5b + 25)x$ during symbolic long division.

questions.title: Autumn 2022 Course Paper 1 · Problem 7
questions.promptMarkdown:
**a)** A second degree polynomial function $f(x)$ has minimal value $-3.5$ and its graph passes through $(75, 4)$ and $(105, 4)$. Determine an expression for $f(x)$.

**b)** A hyperbola function $g(x)$ has horizontal asymptote $y = 100$, vertical asymptote $x = 0$, and $g(5) = 98$. Determine an expression for $g(x)$.
rubricChecks: Find symmetry axis s = (75 + 105)/2 = 90 and write f(x) = a(x - 90)^2 - 3.5
Write g(x) = 100 + a/x and use g(5) = 98 => a = -10 to state g(x) = 100 - 10/x
hints: Hint 1: Equal $y$-values $f(75) = f(105) = 4$ place the axis of symmetry halfway between $75$ and $105$ at $s = 90$ (Ch. 8).
Hint 2: For (b), standard hyperbola form with asymptotes $x = 0$ and $y = 100$ is $g(x) = 100 + \frac{a}{x}$ (Ch. 9).
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**a)** Since $f(75) = f(105) = 4$, the symmetry axis is $x = \frac{75 + 105}{2} = 90$, so $f(x) = a(x - 90)^2 - 3.5$. Substituting $(105, 4)$:
$$a(105 - 90)^2 - 3.5 = 4 \implies 225a = 7.5 \implies a = \frac{7.5}{225} = \frac{1}{30}$$
Hence **$f(x) = \frac{1}{30}(x - 90)^2 - 3.5$**.

**b)** With vertical asymptote $x = 0$ and horizontal asymptote $y = 100$, $g(x) = 100 + \frac{a}{x}$. From $g(5) = 98$: $100 + \frac{a}{5} = 98 \implies a = -10$, so **$g(x) = 100 - \frac{10}{x}$**.
questions.pitfall: Rounding $\frac{1}{30} \approx 0.03$ crudely instead of keeping the exact fraction $\frac{1}{30}$.

questions.title: Autumn 2022 Course Paper 1 · Problem 8
questions.promptMarkdown:
Given the four points $A = (6, 4)$, $B = (10, 4)$, $C = (10, 8)$ and $D = (6, 8)$:

**a)** Determine the equation of the circle that passes through $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$.

**b)** Find the equation of an ellipse with horizontal and vertical symmetry axes that passes through $A, B, C, D$ and is wider than it is tall ($a > b$).

**c)** Decide whether there exists an ellipse with horizontal and vertical symmetry axes that passes through $A, B, C, D$ **and** the origin $(0, 0)$.
rubricChecks: Use symmetry of the square A,B,C,D to find centre (8, 6) and squared radius (10-8)^2 + (8-6)^2 = 8: (x - 8)^2 + (y - 6)^2 = 8
Write ellipse ((x - 8)^2)/a^2 + ((y - 6)^2)/b^2 = 1 requiring 4/a^2 + 4/b^2 = 1 with a > b (e.g. a = 3, b^2 = 7.2)
Test (0, 0): 64/a^2 + 36/b^2 = 1 combined with 4/a^2 + 4/b^2 = 1 gives 28/a^2 = -8, which is impossible since a^2 > 0
hints: Hint 1: Notice $A, B, C, D$ form a $4 \times 4$ axis-aligned square! Any circle or axis-aligned ellipse through all four vertices must have its centre right at the midpoint $(8, 6)$ (Ch. 8).

Hint 2: Substituting $(10, 8)$ into $\frac{(x - 8)^2}{a^2} + \frac{(y - 6)^2}{b^2} = 1$ gives $\frac{4}{a^2} + \frac{4}{b^2} = 1$. For (c), also substitute $(0, 0)$ to get $\frac{64}{a^2} + \frac{36}{b^2} = 1$ and solve the $2 \times 2$ linear system in $u = \frac{1}{a^2}$ and $v = \frac{1}{b^2}$!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**a)** By symmetry of the rectangle/square $A, B, C, D$, the centre is $(x_0, y_0) = \left(\frac{6+10}{2}, \frac{4+8}{2}\right) = (8, 6)$, and $r^2 = (10 - 8)^2 + (8 - 6)^2 = 8$. Circle equation:
$$(x - 8)^2 + (y - 6)^2 = 8$$

**b)** Any axis-aligned ellipse through $A, B, C, D$ has centre $(8, 6)$ and satisfies $\frac{(10 - 8)^2}{a^2} + \frac{(8 - 6)^2}{b^2} = \frac{4}{a^2} + \frac{4}{b^2} = 1$. Choosing $a = 3$ ($a^2 = 9 > 8$) gives $\frac{4}{b^2} = 1 - \frac{4}{9} = \frac{5}{9} \implies b^2 = 7.2 < 9$ ($a > b$):
$$\frac{(x - 8)^2}{9} + \frac{(y - 6)^2}{7.2} = 1$$

**c)** Passing through $(0, 0)$ requires $\frac{64}{a^2} + \frac{36}{b^2} = 1$. Subtracting $9$ times $\left(\frac{4}{a^2} + \frac{4}{b^2} = 1\right)$ gives:
$$\frac{64 - 36}{a^2} = 1 - 9 \implies \frac{28}{a^2} = -8$$
which is impossible since $a^2 > 0$. Thus **no such ellipse exists**.
questions.pitfall: Using diameter $4$ as radius ($r^2 = 16$) instead of distance from $(8, 6)$ to $(10, 8)$ ($r^2 = 2^2 + 2^2 = 8$).

questions.title: Autumn 2022 Course Paper 1 · Problem 9
questions.promptMarkdown:
Determine the inverse function $g(x)$, its domain of definition $D_g$, and its range $R_g$ for:

**a)** $f(x) = 10 + \dfrac{0.2}{x - 3}$ with domain of definition $D_f = \langle 3, \infty\rangle$.

**b)** $f(x) = \ln(10x - x^2)$ with domain of definition $D_f = [1, 5]$.
rubricChecks: Solve (a) to g(x) = 3 + 0.2/(x - 10) with D_g = <10, infinity> and R_g = <3, infinity>
Complete the square in (b): e^y = 10x - x^2 = 25 - (x - 5)^2 => (x - 5)^2 = 25 - e^y
Select negative branch x = 5 - sqrt(25 - e^y) because x in [1, 5] implies x - 5 <= 0
State g(x) = 5 - sqrt(25 - e^x) with D_g = [ln 9, ln 25] and R_g = [1, 5]
hints: Hint 1: In (a), $f$ decreases from $+\infty$ (as $x \to 3^+$) towards $10^+$ (as $x \to \infty$). Solve $y = 10 + \frac{0.2}{x - 3}$ for $x$ (Ch. 10).
Hint 2: In (b), exponentiate $y = \ln(10x - x^2)$ to get $x^2 - 10x = -e^y$, complete the square $(x - 5)^2 = 25 - e^y$, and use $D_f = [1, 5]$ ($x \le 5$) to pick the right $\pm$ sign!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**a)** Solving $y = 10 + \frac{0.2}{x - 3}$: $y - 10 = \frac{0.2}{x - 3} \implies x = 3 + \frac{0.2}{y - 10}$. Thus **$g(x) = 3 + \frac{0.2}{x - 10}$**, with **$D_g = R_f = \langle 10, \infty\rangle$** and **$R_g = D_f = \langle 3, \infty\rangle$**.

**b)** Exponentiating $y = \ln(10x - x^2)$ gives $10x - x^2 = e^y \iff x^2 - 10x + 25 = 25 - e^y \iff (x - 5)^2 = 25 - e^y$.
Because $x \in D_f = [1, 5]$, we have $x - 5 \le 0$, so $x - 5 = -\sqrt{25 - e^y} \implies x = 5 - \sqrt{25 - e^y}$. Swapping $x$ and $y$:
$$g(x) = 5 - \sqrt{25 - e^x}$$
Since $10x - x^2$ increases on $[1, 5]$ from $9$ to $25$, $f$ increases from $\ln 9$ to $\ln 25$, giving **$D_g = [\ln 9, \ln 25]$** and **$R_g = [1, 5]$**.
questions.pitfall: Choosing $+\sqrt{25 - e^x}$ instead of $-\sqrt{25 - e^x}$ in (b), which lands in $[5, 9]$ instead of $D_f = [1, 5]$!

questions.title: Autumn 2022 Course Paper 1 · Problem 10
questions.promptMarkdown: Use the exponent laws and the property that $e^u > 1$ whenever $u > 0$ (and $e^u > 0$ for all $u$) — **without using differentiation** — to prove that $f(x) = e^x$ is strictly increasing on the whole number line.
rubricChecks: Start with arbitrary real numbers x_1 < x_2 so that u = x_2 - x_1 > 0
Apply given property u > 0 => e^{x_2 - x_1} > 1
Multiply both sides by strictly positive e^{x_1} > 0 and use e^{x_1} * e^{x_2 - x_1} = e^{x_2} to conclude e^{x_1} < e^{x_2}
hints: Hint 1: To prove $f$ is strictly increasing directly from the definition, let $x_1 < x_2$ be arbitrary real numbers and show $e^{x_1} < e^{x_2}$ using valid implication steps (Ch. 1 & 10).
Hint 2: Note $x_1 < x_2 \implies x_2 - x_1 > 0$, apply the given fact to $u = x_2 - x_1$, and multiply both sides of the inequality by $e^{x_1} > 0$!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
Let $x_1$ and $x_2$ be arbitrary real numbers with $x_1 < x_2$. Subtracting $x_1$ gives $x_2 - x_1 > 0$.
By the given property ($u > 0 \implies e^u > 1$):
$$e^{x_2 - x_1} > 1$$
Since $e^{x_1} > 0$ for every real $x_1$, multiplying both sides of the inequality by $e^{x_1}$ preserves the direction of the inequality:
$$e^{x_1} \cdot e^{x_2 - x_1} > e^{x_1} \cdot 1 \implies e^{x_1 + (x_2 - x_1)} > e^{x_1} \implies e^{x_2} > e^{x_1}$$
Thus $x_1 < x_2 \implies f(x_1) < f(x_2)$, proving $f(x) = e^x$ is strictly increasing on $\mathbb{R}$.
questions.pitfall: Using $f'(x) = e^x > 0$ when the problem explicitly forbids differentiation, or multiplying an inequality without stating $e^{x_1} > 0$.

questions.title: Spring 2022 Course Paper 1 · Problem 1
questions.promptMarkdown:
Let $a$ be a parameter. Solve each equation for $x$ (stating clearly for which values of $a$ solutions exist):

**a)** $5\ln(x) - a = 0$  
**b)** $\frac{1}{3}e^x - a + 1 = 0$  
**c)** $\dfrac{a}{x - 3} - 5a + 2 = 0$  
**d)** $ax^4 + 1 = 0$
rubricChecks: Solve (a) x = e^{0.2a} for all a in R, and (b) x = ln(3(a - 1)) = ln(a - 1) + ln 3 for a > 1 (no solution if a <= 1)
Solve (c) x = (16a - 6)/(5a - 2) and identify exceptional parameter values a = 0.4 and a = 0 (no solutions)
Solve (d) x^4 = -1/a => x = ±(-a)^{-1/4} for a < 0 (no solution if a >= 0)
hints: Hint 1: Treat $a$ as a fixed constant while isolating $x$, then inspect every division by an expression in $a$, logarithm argument, or even root for exceptional values of $a$ (Ch. 1 & 5)!
Hint 2: In (c), check **both** $5a - 2 = 0$ ($a = 0.4$) AND $a = 0$ (plug $a = 0$ into the original equation: $0 - 0 + 2 = 0$ is false, or notice $x = \frac{-6}{-2} = 3$ violates $x \ne 3$!).
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**a)** $\ln(x) = \frac{a}{5} \iff \mathbf{x = e^{a/5} = e^{0.2a}}$ (one solution for all $a \in \mathbb{R}$).

**b)** $e^x = 3(a - 1)$. Since $e^x > 0$, **no solution if $a \le 1$**, and **$x = \ln(3(a - 1)) = \ln(a - 1) + \ln 3$ if $a > 1$**.

**c)** Domain requires $x \ne 3$. Rewriting $\frac{a}{x - 3} = 5a - 2$:
- If $a = 0$: original equation becomes $2 = 0$ (**no solution**).
- If $a = 0.4$ ($5a - 2 = 0$): equation becomes $\frac{0.4}{x - 3} = 0$ (**no solution**).
- If $a \ne 0$ and $a \ne 0.4$: $x - 3 = \frac{a}{5a - 2} \implies \mathbf{x = 3 + \frac{a}{5a - 2} = \frac{16a - 6}{5a - 2}}$ (since $\frac{a}{5a - 2} \ne 0$, $x \ne 3$ holds).

**d)** $ax^4 = -1$. If $a \ge 0$, $ax^4 \ge 0 \ne -1$ (**no solution**). If $a < 0$, $x^4 = -\frac{1}{a} > 0 \implies \mathbf{x = \pm(-a)^{-1/4}}$.
questions.pitfall: Missing $a = 0$ as an exceptional case in (c): plugging $a = 0$ into $x = \frac{16a - 6}{5a - 2}$ gives $x = 3$, which makes the original denominator $x - 3 = 0$!

questions.title: Spring 2022 Course Paper 1 · Problem 2
questions.promptMarkdown:
Let $a$ be a parameter. Solve each inequality for $x$:

**a)** $\frac{1}{5}\ln(x - a) \le 1$  
**b)** $ax + x \ge 1$  
**c)** $\dfrac{x - a}{x - 3} + 2 \ge 0$  
**d)** $e^{x - a} \le a$
rubricChecks: Include log domain x > a in (a) to get a < x <= a + e^5
Split (b) (a + 1)x >= 1 into three cases: a > -1 (x >= 1/(a+1)), a < -1 (x <= 1/(a+1)), and a = -1 (no solutions)
Combine (c) into (3x - a - 6)/(x - 3) >= 0 and split cases a < 3, a = 3 (all x ≠ 3), and a > 3
Split (d) into a <= 0 (no solutions) and a > 0 (x <= a + ln a)
hints: Hint 1: Whenever you divide an inequality by a parameter expression like $(a + 1)$, split into $> 0$, $= 0$, and $< 0$ cases because dividing by a negative flips $\ge$ to $\le$ (Ch. 5 & 7)!
Hint 2: In (c), combine over $x - 3$ as $\frac{3x - (a + 6)}{x - 3} \ge 0$: compare the numerator root $x = \frac{a + 6}{3}$ against the denominator root $x = 3$ (they collide when $a = 3$!).
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**a)** Requires $x - a > 0 \iff x > a$. Multiplying by $5$ and exponentiating: $\ln(x - a) \le 5 \iff x - a \le e^5$, so **$a < x \le a + e^5$**.

**b)** Rewrite as $(a + 1)x \ge 1$:
- If $a > -1$: **$x \ge \frac{1}{a + 1}$**.
- If $a = -1$: $0 \ge 1$, **no solutions**.
- If $a < -1$: **$x \le \frac{1}{a + 1}$**.

**c)** Combine over $x - 3$: $\frac{x - a + 2(x - 3)}{x - 3} = \frac{3x - a - 6}{x - 3} \ge 0$. Comparing root $\frac{a + 6}{3}$ with $3$:
- If $a < 3$ ($\frac{a+6}{3} < 3$): **$x \le \frac{a + 6}{3}$ or $x > 3$**.
- If $a = 3$: $\frac{3(x - 3)}{x - 3} = 3 \ge 0$ for **all $x \ne 3$**.
- If $a > 3$ ($\frac{a+6}{3} > 3$): **$x < 3$ or $x \ge \frac{a + 6}{3}$**.

**d)** Since $e^{x - a} > 0$: if $a \le 0$, **no solutions**; if $a > 0$, $x - a \le \ln a \iff \mathbf{x \le a + \ln a}$.
questions.pitfall: Forgetting the strict lower bound $x > a$ in (a), or forgetting that the order of the two critical points $\frac{a+6}{3}$ and $3$ flips at $a = 3$ in (c).

questions.title: Spring 2022 Course Paper 1 · Problem 3
questions.promptMarkdown:
Consider the cash flow with discount rate $15\%$:

| Year | $0$ | $2$ | $8$ | $9$ | $10$ |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Payment | $-60$ | $-60$ | $80$ | $80$ | $80$ |

**a)** Calculate the present value of the cash flow.

**b)** Calculate the future value of the cash flow after $7$ years.

**c)** Suggest an extra payment after $7$ years such that the internal rate of return (IRR) of the modified cash flow becomes $15\%$.
rubricChecks: Propose extra inflow +97.62 at year 7 so FV_7 = 0 => PV(0.15) = 0 => IRR = 15%
hints: Hint 1: Discount each payment by $1.15^t$ using exact years $t \in \{0, 2, 8, 9, 10\}$, then multiply $\text{PV}$ by $1.15^7$ to get $\text{FV}_7$ (Ch. 3).
Hint 2: An extra payment $X$ at year $7$ adds $X$ directly to $\text{FV}_7$; since $\text{PV} = \text{FV}_7 / 1.15^7$, making $\text{FV}_7 = 0$ makes $15\%$ an IRR!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**a)** Present value at $r = 15\%$:
$$\text{PV} = -60 - \frac{60}{1.15^2} + \frac{80}{1.15^8} + \frac{80}{1.15^9} + \frac{80}{1.15^{10}} \approx -36.70$$

**b)** Future value after $7$ years:
$$\text{FV}_7 = \text{PV} \cdot 1.15^7 \approx -36.6976 \cdot 1.15^7 \approx -97.62$$

**c)** Adding an extra payment of **$+97.62$** after $7$ years makes the new year-$7$ future value $-97.62 + 97.62 = 0$, which implies $\text{NPV}(0.15) = \frac{0}{1.15^7} = 0$, so **$15\%$ is the IRR**.
questions.pitfall: Discounting $+97.62$ a second time when answering (c): the payment happens **at year $7$**, where the shortfall is $-97.62$!

questions.title: Spring 2022 Course Paper 1 · Problem 4
questions.promptMarkdown:
**a)** Calculate the present value of $60$ million paid in $7$ years at $9\%$ annual interest.

**b)** Interpret the present value from (a) as a bank deposit.

**c–d)** Suppose instead the $60$ million is paid in $6$ years. Determine the annual interest rate $r$ that gives the **same** present value as in (a).
rubricChecks: Calculate PV = 60 / 1.09^7 ≈ 32.82 million
Interpret 32.82 million as the amount deposited today at 9% annual interest that grows to 60 million in 7 years
hints: Hint 1: Present value of $K$ in $t$ years at annual rate $r$ is $\frac{K}{(1 + r)^t}$ (Ch. 2 & 3).
Hint 2: Set $\frac{60}{(1 + r)^6} = \frac{60}{1.09^7}$ so $(1 + r)^6 = 1.09^7$ — solve exact powers before rounding!
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**a)** $\text{PV} = \frac{60}{1.09^7} \approx \mathbf{32.82\text{ million}}$.

**b)** If you deposit $32.82$ million in an account today earning $9\%$ annual interest, the balance after $7$ years will be $32.82 \cdot 1.09^7 = 60$ million.

**c–d)** Requiring equal present values gives:
$$\frac{60}{(1 + r)^6} = \frac{60}{1.09^7} \iff (1 + r)^6 = 1.09^7 \iff r = 1.09^{7/6} - 1 \approx 0.1058 = \mathbf{10.58\%}$$
questions.pitfall: Approximating $r \approx 9\% \cdot \frac{7}{6} = 10.50\%$ linearly instead of solving $(1 + r)^6 = 1.09^7$ ($10.58\%$).
